topic.name: Simple Fraction Sums
topic.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7)
evidence: Calculate 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5
Calculate 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8
Explain that when denominators are the same, you add/subtract the numerators
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 2/8 of a cup of milk and then another 3/8 of a cup, can {{name}} work out the total without a calculator?

pedagogy.summary: The first fraction operation: adding and subtracting fractions that share a denominator, staying within one whole (5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7). The whole idea is that the denominator NAMES the unit (sevenths) and stays fixed, while the numerators COUNT how many of that unit and are combined like whole numbers. Taught well, it is simply counting like things: two fifths and two fifths make four fifths, exactly as two apples and two apples make four apples — the 'apple' here is the fifth. The denominator is not a number to operate on; it is the label of what is being counted.
bestPractices: Present it as counting like units — use 'dual naming' ('three one-fifths and one one-fifth make four one-fifths' alongside '3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5') so the denominator is heard as the unit being counted, not a second number.
Hold the whole and the unit constant with a single partitioned bar or fraction strip so pieces are visibly the same size and only the count changes.
Keep to same denominators and results within one whole first; establish which of a pair is bigger before adding, per NFER.
Confront the add-across error early and directly (2/5 + 2/5 is not 4/10) using a model where the denominator cannot change.
Do subtraction alongside addition as separating the same units (6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8), keeping the eighth as the fixed unit.
keyRepresentations: Fraction strip / bar partitioned into the fixed unit (sevenths, eighths) where pieces are combined or removed
Number line marked in the unit fraction, counting on/back in that unit
Discrete 'like objects' framing (each piece = one unit fraction) to make combining feel like counting
Paper folded/cut into equal parts (NFER's cut-a-strip-into-sevenths)
commonMisconceptions: Adds (or subtracts) the denominators as well as the numerators: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/10, misapplying whole-number addition (IES; ~10% of lower-achieving Y6 on an easy same-denominator item, NFER).
Drops the unit and answers a bare whole number: 6/8 − 3/8 = 3, operating only on the numerators as if the denominator weren't there.
Treats the denominator as a quantity to be operated on rather than the name of the unit being counted.

learn.summary: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7, 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8). The core idea: the denominator NAMES the unit being counted (sevenths, eighths) and stays fixed, while the numerators COUNT how many of that unit and are combined like whole numbers — 'two fifths and two fifths make four fifths' just as two apples and two apples make four apples, where the 'apple' is the fifth. Teaching targets two misconceptions: adding the denominators too (2/5 + 2/5 → 4/10) and dropping the unit to give a bare whole number (6/8 − 3/8 → 3). For ages 7–8.

activities.title: Locked-unit bar combiner (fixed-denominator model)
feedback: If a learner expects 4/10, have them lay four tenth-pieces next to the built sum. They cover only two fifths, less than the four fifths already on the bar, so 4/10 is too small. Counting the fifths gives 4/5.
If a learner wants to write a bare whole number for 6/8 − 3/8, point back to the eighths bar: three eighth-pieces remain, so the answer is 3/8, measured in eighths, not 3.
Read each piece aloud as 'one fifth' (or 'one eighth') so the denominator is heard as the name of the unit, not a second number.
activities.rationale: Combining visibly same-size pieces on a model where the unit is held constant makes the count change while the unit cannot, directly confronting the add-across error. A placing/snapping interaction with a live running count and spoken piece-naming makes the counting mechanism concrete. (The moment where four tenths visibly cover less than the 4/5 sum is a model affordance; its effectiveness against the misconception is not established by the cited sources.)
sourceClaims: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
learnerActions: Work with a bar already partitioned into a fixed unit, e.g. fifths, with the label 'fifths' shown on the bar.
Combine 2/5 and another 2/5 by placing the pieces onto the bar; watch a running count read '4/5' as each piece is read aloud as 'one fifth'.

Test the answer '4/10' by laying four tenth-sized pieces next to the 4/5 you built. Notice that they cover only as much as two fifths, which is less than the four fifths on the bar, so 4/10 is the wrong amount. The pieces you are counting are all fifths.
Switch to subtraction on an eighths bar and remove pieces: start with 6/8 and take away 3/8, reading off 3/8 left.
Try adding one 2/5 too many and watch it run past the end of the bar, foreshadowing sums beyond one whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When denominators are the same, you are counting same-size pieces, so only the count (numerator) changes and the unit (denominator) stays fixed.

activities.title: Dual naming — read fractions as repeated unit fractions
feedback: If a learner starts to combine the denominators, re-voice the sum as 'how many one-fifths altogether?' to pull attention back to counting units.
Praise answers that keep the unit named: 'four one-fifths' is exactly 4/5.
activities.rationale: Hearing the denominator as the unit being counted may reduce the chance of mistakenly operating on it. Dual naming is offered as a supporting verbal routine to accompany the model work; the supporting source is marked unverified in the row.
sourceClaims: Securing that a non-unit fraction is a repeated sum of unit fractions ('three one-fifths'), via dual naming, minimises the chance of children mistakenly operating on the denominator.
learnerActions: Say each fraction two ways: 'three one-fifths' alongside '3/5', and 'one one-fifth' alongside '1/5'.
State the sum both ways: 'three one-fifths and one one-fifth make four one-fifths' alongside '3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5'.
Do the same for subtraction: 'six one-eighths take away three one-eighths leaves three one-eighths', alongside '6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8'.
Point to the denominator each time and name it as the unit being counted.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-unit fraction is a repeated sum of unit fractions, so adding/subtracting is counting those units up or down — the denominator is the label, not a quantity to operate on.

activities.title: Number line counting in the unit fraction
feedback: If the answer comes out as a whole number like 3, re-anchor: 6/8 and 3/8 are points on the line and the gap between them is measured in eighths, so 3/8.
If a sum of two pieces came out smaller than one piece, that's a signal to recheck — adding two pieces should give more, not less.
activities.rationale: A number line re-anchors the fraction as a quantity measured in the unit, specifically countering the 'drop the unit, answer a whole number' error. Estimation (bigger/smaller than a piece) exposes implausible answers.
sourceClaims: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
learnerActions: Mark a number line in the unit fraction (e.g. eighths) from 0 to 1.
For 6/8 − 3/8, land on 6/8, count back 3 eighths, and read where you stop (3/8).
For a sum, start at one fraction and count on in the unit, reading each step.
State whether the answer is bigger or smaller than one of the pieces and check your result against that expectation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fractions are quantities/points measured in the unit; combining them is counting on or back in that unit, and the answer is still a count of eighths (6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8, not 3).

activities.title: Paper strip folded/cut into equal parts
feedback: If a learner reaches for a differently-sized piece, compare it against the cut pieces — it isn't a seventh, so it can't be part of this count.
Count the pieces together out loud to confirm the numerator while naming the unit.
activities.rationale: Hands-on cutting and counting of equal paper parts builds part-of-whole understanding through a different concrete medium than a screen model. Real paper pieces have slight thickness and are an approximation of the idealised flat equal parts; neither the paper nor the screen bar is uniquely necessary.
sourceClaims: On an easy same-denominator addition, 92% of Year 6 pupils were correct, but ~10% of lower-achieving pupils added both numerators and denominators (6/7 → 6/14); NFER recommends concrete materials (cut a strip into sevenths) to build part-of-whole understanding.
learnerActions: Fold and cut a paper strip into the fixed unit, e.g. sevenths (or eighths), so every piece is the same size.
Build 5/7 + 1/7 by gathering pieces and counting them: six sevenths, 6/7.
Build 6/8 − 3/8 by setting out six eighth-pieces and removing three, leaving 3/8.
Say aloud what each piece is called and how many there are after combining or removing.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically counting identical cut parts makes clear that combining fractions of the same denominator is counting like units; the piece size (unit) never changes.

activities.title: Fluency practice and error-baiting check (companion)
feedback: If 5/16 is chosen, remind: the denominator names the piece size and stays 8; count the eighths — 5/8.
If 5 is chosen, remind: the answer is measured in eighths, so 5/8, not 5.
Ask the learner to show the answer on a strip to confirm their choice.
activities.rationale: Scored practice is efficient for rehearsing fluency and can probe the misconceptions with targeted distractors, but it elicits recognition/a final answer rather than independent construction of the combining, so it is a companion to the model work.
sourceClaims: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in items such as '2/5 + 2/5 = _/_' and '6/8 − 3/8 = _/_'.
Choose the correct answer to 3/8 + 2/8 from options that include 5/16 (add-across error) and 5 (bare whole number) as distractors, and say why each wrong option is wrong.
Shade pieces on a strip to match each sum or difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Same-denominator sums and differences can be rehearsed to fluency, and deliberately including the add-across and dropped-unit answers as distractors checks whether the unit idea is secure.

constraints: Keep to same denominators with results within one whole first; establish which of a pair is bigger before adding.
Confront the add-across error (2/5 + 2/5 ≠ 4/10) and the dropped-unit error (6/8 − 3/8 ≠ 3) early and directly, using models where the denominator cannot change.
Do subtraction alongside addition as separating the same units, keeping the unit fraction fixed; don't assess only one operation, which lets a learner pass on a lucky case.

A static tap-to-reveal strip (labelling numerator vs denominator, showing one worked sum) can serve as a reference anchor but does not let the learner combine pieces themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main doing.
Scored quiz items elicit recognition or a final answer, not independent construction of the combining, so pair them with construction on a model.
Paper/card pieces have real thickness and are an approximation of ideal flat equal parts; a screen bar is an idealised model — both are usable, neither is uniquely necessary.
Compare fractions by holding the common unit (denominator) fixed and counting the numerators; the denominator is a fixed label of the unit, not a quantity that is operated on or 'flipped'.

probeDeeper: Why does the bottom number stay 5 when you add two fifths?
Show me 2/5 + 2/5 on a strip or number line — where do you land?
A friend says 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16. Work out what 6/16 is — is it bigger or smaller than 3/8? Can adding two pieces give you the same as just one of them?
If you add two pieces together, should the answer be bigger or smaller than one piece? Check your answer against that.
assess.correctAnswer: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5 (denominator stays fifths, add the counts 2 + 2). 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8 (denominator stays eighths, 6 − 3 = 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts the denominators as well: '2 and 2 is 4 on top, 5 and 5 is 10 on the bottom, so 4/10' — operates on the denominator as if it were a second whole number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a fixed-unit strip: 2/5 and 2/5 are four SAME-SIZE fifth-pieces, so the answer is fifths; the fifth (denominator) names the piece and can't change when you just count more of them. Contrast tenths physically not fitting the fifths bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 4/10 for the sum (or does 8−8 / 6−6 on the bottom in the subtraction); the denominator changes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the unit and gives a whole number: '6 take away 3 is 3' — answers 3, operating only on the numerators and losing the eighths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the fraction as a number/quantity on a number line: 6/8 and 3/8 are points, and their difference is still measured in eighths; shade 6 eighths, remove 3, read what's left — 3 eighths, not 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Final answer written as a whole number (3) rather than 3/8; the denominator disappears from the answer.

responseLevels.gap: Operates on the denominator too (4/10) or drops the unit and answers a whole number (3); cannot combine same-size parts as a count.
responseLevels.full: Adds and subtracts the numerators while keeping the denominator fixed (4/5, 3/8) and can justify or show it as counting like unit fractions (two fifths and two fifths make four fifths), transferring cleanly to a fresh same-denominator pair.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the same-denominator addition right by rule (4/5) but applies the numerator rule mechanically — falters on the subtraction, can't show it on a model, or is unsure why the denominator stays the same.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two to work out — show me each step as you go, out loud or on paper: 2/5 + 2/5, and 6/8 − 3/8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands they are counting like units keeps the denominator fixed and combines only the numerators — 4/5 and 3/8. Watching the working (not just the final number) exposes the two failure modes a correct reasoner never shows: changing the denominator too (4/10, 3/0) reveals the fraction isn't seen as a fixed-size unit, and answering a bare '3' reveals the unit has been dropped entirely. Doing both an addition and a subtraction with the same fixed unit stops a child passing on one lucky case.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
topic.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, including results greater than one whole (e.g. 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8)
evidence: Calculate 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 and explain it equals 1 2/5
Subtract 2/6 from 5/6
Solve addition problems where the sum exceeds the whole: 7/8 + 3/8
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 5/8 of a bag of flour and then another 6/8, can {{name}} work out the total and explain what the answer means as a mixed number?

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions where the result can pass one whole (3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5). The same counting-like-units idea as within one whole, extended by one crucial step: when the numerators combine past the denominator, the extra units re-group into a whole. Seven fifths is a legitimate number; eight eighths make one whole, and ten eighths is one whole and two eighths. The teaching work is making children comfortable that a fraction can exceed one, and fluent at re-unitising the improper result into a mixed number.
bestPractices: Keep the counting-like-units foundation ('seven one-fifths') and simply let the count exceed the denominator, so the improper fraction arises naturally from adding.
Use two adjacent whole-bars so pieces spilling past the first whole are visibly re-grouped into 1 and a remainder — making 7/5 = 1 2/5 something the child sees, not a trick.
Name the improper fraction as legitimate ('7/5 is a real number, more than one') to head off the belief that fractions must be less than a whole.
Teach improper↔mixed conversion as counting how many whole-groups of the denominator fit, using the model before the numeric rule.
Do subtraction across the whole too (from a mixed/improper start) as separating like units.
keyRepresentations: Two (or more) partitioned whole-bars side by side, pieces spilling from one into the next
Number line extending past 1, counting on in the unit fraction (fifths past 5/5)
Ten-frame-style grouping where a full set of denominator-many pieces fuses into one whole
Improper↔mixed toggle on the same shaded quantity (10/8 ↔ 1 2/8)
commonMisconceptions: Adds the denominators as well: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10 (add-across; on harder items this error spreads into middle-achieving pupils, NFER).
Believes a fraction cannot exceed one whole, so forces the result — stops at 5/5 = 1, or flips 7/5 to 5/7 — rather than accepting an improper fraction.
Miscounts the re-grouping when converting improper to mixed (e.g. 7/5 = 2 2/5 or 1 3/5), losing track of how many wholes the denominator makes.

learn.summary: Teaches adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions where the result can pass one whole (e.g. 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5). Extends the counting-like-units idea by one step: when the combined count passes the denominator, the extra unit fractions re-group into a whole. Core aims are making children comfortable that a fraction can legitimately exceed one, and fluent at re-unitising an improper result into a mixed number. Addresses the add-across error (3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10), the belief that fractions cannot exceed one, and miscounting the re-group when converting. Covers subtraction too, both within one whole and crossing it from a mixed/improper start.

activities.title: Spilling into the next whole: an adding model across two bars
feedback: If the child writes 7/10 for 3/5 + 4/5 (or 10/16 for 7/8 + 3/8): return to the fixed-unit bar — 3/5 and 4/5 are seven same-size fifth-pieces, so the answer is in fifths; only the count grows (likewise 7/8 + 3/8 is ten eighths). Point out that the pieces on the bar are fifths, not tenths, and that 7/10 is less than one whole even though seven fifths fill more than one bar.

If the child flips 7/5 to 5/7, caps the answer at 1, or refuses to write 7/5: show the count continuing past 5/5 on the bars and on a number line; fifths keep coming after one whole, and 7/5 is a real number just past one. Name it as 'more than one whole' before converting.

If the addition is correct but the mixed number is wrong (e.g. 7/5 = 2 2/5 or 1 3/5): do not reteach adding — it is right. Ask how many fifths make ONE whole, so how many whole groups fit inside 7/5, and what is left over; count the whole-groups on the bar.
If a crossing-the-whole subtraction stalls (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5): show that one whole can be re-grouped into fifths (1 1/5 = 6/5), so there are now six fifths to take three from, leaving 3/5.
activities.rationale: A multi-bar fixed-unit model lets the re-grouping at the whole be observed directly, so the mixed number arises from the count passing the denominator rather than from a symbolic rule. Keeping the denominator locked targets the add-across error by showing the unit cannot change. The number line and 'name it as legitimate' step directly confront the belief that fractions cannot exceed one.
sourceClaims: The add-across error (adding numerators and denominators) stems from misapplying whole-number addition and not treating fractions as numbers with magnitude; teach why the procedure works with fixed-unit models and estimation.
Understanding a fraction a/b (a>1) as a repeated sum of unit fractions underpins accepting improper fractions and converting to mixed numbers.
learnerActions: Set up two identical bars side by side, each partitioned into the SAME fixed unit (e.g. eighths), with the denominator kept locked so only the count of pieces changes.
Add 7/8 + 3/8 by placing eighth-pieces: fill the first bar with eight eighths, then let the remaining two eighths land in the second bar.
When a full set of denominator-many pieces (eight eighths) completes the first bar, group that full set into a single 'one whole' tile, so the child watches the whole form from the count.
Read the quantity both ways on the same shaded amount: as an improper fraction 10/8 and as a mixed number 1 2/8.
Repeat with 3/5 + 4/5: count fifths past 5/5 and re-group 7/5 as 1 2/5.

Do subtraction too: a within-whole case (5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6) where like units are simply separated, and a genuine crossing-the-whole case from a mixed/improper start that requires re-grouping a whole back into unit fractions (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5 = 6/5 − 3/5 = 3/5), treating both as separating like units.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction can exceed one whole; when the running count of unit fractions reaches the denominator those pieces re-group into one whole, which is how an improper fraction becomes a mixed number — seen, not memorised. Subtraction reverses the same re-grouping when a whole must be broken back into unit fractions.

activities.title: Counting on past one whole on a number line
feedback: If the child stops at 1 (5/5) and will not continue: emphasise the ticks keep going; fifths after 5/5 are 6/5, 7/5 and so on.
If the child lands on the wrong tick: recount the unit steps one at a time, saying each unit-fraction name aloud.
activities.rationale: A number line makes magnitude explicit and gives a second representation of crossing one whole, complementing the area bars and reinforcing that an improper fraction is a genuine position on the line.
sourceClaims: Understanding a fraction a/b (a>1) as a repeated sum of unit fractions underpins accepting improper fractions and converting to mixed numbers.
learnerActions: Mark a number line from 0 extending past 1, with tick marks at each unit fraction (fifths past 5/5).
Place 3/5, then count on four more fifth-steps (4/5 in total), landing at 7/5 and noting where the count crossed the 1 mark.
State how many unit steps are before 1 and how many are after, reading off the mixed number 1 2/5.
Repeat for 7/8 + 3/8, identifying the point where the total passes one whole.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding same-denominator fractions is counting on in the unit fraction; passing the '1' mark shows concretely that the result is more than one whole and where the mixed-number remainder comes from.

activities.title: Check and explain: improper and mixed forms
feedback: If the child accepts 10/16 as larger than 7/8 without question: point out 10/16 simplifies to 5/8, which is SMALLER than 7/8 — adding two positive amounts cannot make the total smaller, which exposes the add-across error.
If the child gives the correct improper fraction but a wrong mixed number: ask how many of the unit fraction make one whole, then count the whole-groups on the model before applying any rule.
If the child gives a correct answer: ask them to check it against the bar or number line and state where the count passed one whole.
activities.rationale: Checkable items that demand both forms and a size comparison surface the two key misconceptions and the conversion slip. Using a magnitude/estimation check is directly recommended for the add-across error. Recognition and matching here consolidate the model but do not by themselves demonstrate independent construction — pair with the production required in the first activity.
sourceClaims: The add-across error (adding numerators and denominators) stems from misapplying whole-number addition and not treating fractions as numbers with magnitude; teach why the procedure works with fixed-unit models and estimation.
learnerActions: Work out 3/5 + 4/5 and 7/8 + 3/8, writing each answer first as an improper fraction and then as a mixed number, showing each step.
Match improper fractions to their mixed-number equivalents on the same shaded quantity (e.g. 10/8 ↔ 1 2/8).
Explain in words why the denominator stays fixed while the count grows.
Respond to a friend's claim that 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/16: simplify 10/16, compare its size with 7/8, and judge whether adding could make the total smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Requiring both the improper and mixed form, plus a magnitude check, reveals whether the child can re-group the whole or is only manipulating symbols; adding two positive same-denominator fractions cannot shrink the total below either addend.

constraints: Keep the denominator locked in all models so the unit stays fixed; this is what makes the add-across error visible as a change of unit.

A single static worked example can display one crossing-the-whole case and an improper↔mixed pair as an anchor, but it does not let the child perform the re-grouping; use it only as a reference alongside an activity where the child acts.

Matching and multiple-choice items consolidate and check, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction; include tasks where the child writes and explains both forms themselves.

Introduce the numeric improper↔mixed conversion rule only after the child has done the re-grouping on a model; the model-before-rule ordering is the intended sequence, not a claim that a rule-first approach can never work.

Include subtraction that crosses the whole (from mixed/improper starts) as well as within-whole subtraction, since the objective covers both; crossing-the-whole subtraction must actually start from or pass one whole (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5), unlike 5/6 − 2/6 which stays within one whole.

Answer options that 'cap at one whole' or flip the improper fraction are useful bait for the can't-exceed-one belief, but ensure the correct answer and feedback explicitly validate the improper fraction as a real number.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Back to the fixed-unit bar: 3/5 and 4/5 are seven same-size fifth-pieces, so the answer is fifths; only the count grows. Contrast that tenths won't fit the fifths bar.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a fraction can't be bigger than one whole, so forces the answer — 'you can't have 7/5, so it's 5/7' or 'it just makes 1'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the count continuing past the whole on a number line and on two bars — fifths keep coming after 5/5; 7/5 is a real number just past one. Name it explicitly as more than one whole before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Flips the improper fraction (7/5→5/7), caps the answer at 1, or refuses to write 7/5; discomfort when the count exceeds the denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds correctly but miscounts the re-group: '7/5 = 2 2/5' or '1 3/5' — loses track of how many wholes the denominator makes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach adding — it's correct. Scaffold the conversion on the model: how many fifths make ONE whole? So how many wholes are in 7/5, and what's left over? Count the whole-groups on the bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct improper fraction (7/5) but a wrong mixed number; the addition is sound, only the conversion slips.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across the denominators (7/10) and/or refuses or mangles the result greater than one (5/7, caps at 1); cannot re-group past the whole.
responseLevels.full: Adds keeping the denominator fixed, accepts 7/5 / 10/8 as legitimate, re-groups into 1 2/5 / 1 2/8, and explains it as counting fifths/eighths past a whole; transfers to a new sum that crosses one whole.
responseLevels.partial: Adds the numerators correctly to the improper fraction (7/5, 10/8) but can't reliably convert to a mixed number, or is uneasy that the answer exceeds one — has the numerator rule but not the re-unitising at the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing each step: 3/5 + 4/5, and 7/8 + 3/8. Write each answer as an improper fraction and then as a mixed number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both sums are engineered to exceed one whole, so a child who believes fractions can't pass one is forced to reveal it — they flip 7/5 to 5/7, stop at 5/5 = 1, or balk. Add-across produces 7/10 / 10/16 (denominator changed). Requiring the answer both as an improper fraction and as a mixed number surfaces whether the child can re-group the whole or only manipulate symbols. Watching the working shows whether the unit is held fixed and re-unitised at the whole.

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers with like denominators has two viable routes: operate on the whole-number and fraction parts separately, or convert both to improper fractions. The separate-parts route exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5 needs regrouping to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the minuend's fraction can be smaller than the subtrahend's, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6). The convert-to-improper route sidesteps the borrow entirely, which is exactly why it is worth teaching as the fallback. Teach both, let the awkward subtraction MOTIVATE the improper method, and keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH methods and let a subtraction that needs regrouping (4 2/6 − 1 5/6) motivate why converting to improper fractions is often cleaner
Make the borrow physical: exchange one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6) before subtracting the fraction parts
In addition, always check whether the fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup (7/5 → 1 2/5) so the answer is a proper mixed number
Estimate with the whole numbers first (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 is between 3 and 5, near 4½) to police the result
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit — fifths add to fifths — to block the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits
keyRepresentations: Number line: jump the whole numbers, then the fraction parts, crossing whole boundaries
Bar model with whole tiles plus fraction tiles; a whole tile that shatters into b unit-fractions for the borrow, or b fraction tiles that fuse into a whole
The regroup written as 4 = 3 + 6/6 (or the improper rewrite 26/6)
Improper-fraction form beside the mixed form for comparison
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the fraction parts (3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10), applying whole-number addition to numerator and denominator
Subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never borrows (4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5|=3)
Leaves an improper fraction part in the answer (3 7/5) instead of regrouping to 4 2/5
Miscounts when converting mixed to improper (2 3/5 → 10/5 then forgets the +3/5, or writes 5/5)

learn.summary: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators (ages 9–10). Two routes are worth teaching: (a) operate on whole-number and fraction parts separately, which exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5, regroup to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the first fraction can be smaller than the second, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6); and (b) convert both to improper fractions, which sidesteps the borrow and is worth teaching as the cleaner fallback. Let the awkward subtraction motivate the improper method, keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout, and always tidy an improper fraction part back into a proper mixed number.

activities.title: Trade a whole for unit fractions: make the borrow and carry physical
feedback: If you take |2 − 5| = 3 and write 3 3/6, you subtracted the smaller fraction from the larger without exchanging. Trade one whole for 6 sixths first so you have 8 sixths to subtract from — or convert both to improper fractions (26/6 − 11/6).
If you write 3/5 + 4/5 as 7/10, you added the denominators too. Three fifths and four fifths is seven fifths: the size of the part does not change when you join same-size parts.
If you leave 3 7/5, check: is 7/5 more than a whole? Tidy it into the whole-number part to get 4 2/5. Your addition itself was correct.
activities.rationale: Making the regroup a felt exchange of one whole for its unit fractions targets the add-across and never-borrow misconceptions directly and keeps the denominator as a fixed unit. Locked fraction tiles make the add-across error impossible during the manipulation; the number line offers a parallel view of the same crossing.
sourceClaims: The add-across misconception (adding numerators AND denominators) is a central, documented error in fraction addition/subtraction, arising from misapplying whole-number addition and failing to treat the denominator as the size of the part.

Same-denominator addition items are answered correctly by the large majority (~92%) but a minority of lower-attaining pupils add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and 'which is bigger' reasoning support remediation.
learnerActions: Work the subtraction 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 using whole tiles and fraction tiles that are locked to sixths so you cannot change the denominator.
Try to take away 5 sixths when you only have 2 — notice you are stuck. Break one whole tile into 6 sixths (the borrow), so you now have 8 sixths, and finish: 8/6 − 5/6 = 3/6, leaving 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Work the addition 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 the same way: gather the fifths, and when 5 fifths collect, fuse them into a fresh whole tile, giving 4 2/5.

Optionally model the same two problems on a number line: jump the whole numbers first, then the fraction parts, and watch a jump cross a whole boundary — the same regroup seen as a different representation.
Write each exchange as a number sentence: 4 = 3 + 6/6, and 7/5 = 1 + 2/5.
Say aloud whether the carry and the borrow are the same exchange running in opposite directions.
activities.intendedInsight: Borrowing is not a mysterious digit-move: it is literally trading one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6), and carrying is the reverse — fusing a whole-worth of unit fractions back into one whole. The denominator stays fixed because fifths only join with fifths.

activities.title: The improper-fraction fallback, side by side
feedback: If your two methods disagree, check the improper conversion: 2 wholes of fifths is 10/5, and you still add the 3/5 on top.
If you write 2 3/5 as 10/5, you forgot to add the 3/5 — it should be 13/5.

Standards expect pupils to add and subtract mixed numbers by replacing each with an equivalent (improper) fraction and/or by using properties of operations, so being fluent in both routes is the goal.
activities.rationale: The subtraction that needs a borrow is the natural motivation for the improper method; running both side by side lets learners compare and self-check. Miscounting during conversion is a known error to guard against.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction' (4.NF.B.3c). In England, adding/subtracting mixed numbers using equivalent fractions is a Year 6 objective.
learnerActions: Rewrite 4 2/6 and 1 5/6 as improper fractions (26/6 and 11/6), subtract to get 15/6, then convert back: 15/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Do the same subtraction by the separate-parts borrow method and check both answers match.
When converting 2 3/5 to improper, count carefully: 2 wholes is 10/5, plus 3/5 is 13/5 — do not drop the +3/5 or stop at 5/5.
Decide which method you found cleaner for the subtraction, and explain why converting to improper removed the borrow.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting to improper fractions avoids the borrow entirely, so it is a reliable fallback when the subtraction needs regrouping; both methods give the same answer when done carefully.

activities.title: Estimate first to police the answer
feedback: If your answer is far from the estimate, re-check for a missed borrow or for added denominators. Separately, check that the fraction part is proper; an untidied part like 3 7/5 has the right value but still needs regrouping to 4 2/5.
3 7/5 is not a tidy mixed number because 7/5 is more than a whole; regroup it to 4 2/5.
activities.rationale: Estimating with the whole numbers and then adjusting for the fraction parts gives learners an independent reasonableness check against value errors such as a missed borrow or added denominators. The proper-fraction check covers un-regrouped answers, which have the correct value.
learnerActions: Before computing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, estimate using the whole numbers: the sum is between 3 and 5, and since both fraction parts are large, near 4 1/2.
Compute the exact answer and check it sits close to your estimate.

Repeat for 4 2/6 − 1 5/6: whole-number subtraction gives about 3, but because 2/6 is less than 5/6 the fraction part pulls the answer down by about a half, so expect a result between 2 and 3, around 2 1/2 — then confirm 2 1/2 is reasonable.
For each result, ask: is the fraction part proper (numerator less than denominator)? If not, regroup.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate that starts with the whole numbers and then adjusts for the fraction parts catches value errors such as a missed borrow (3 3/6 instead of about 2 1/2) or added denominators (3 7/10 instead of about 4 1/2), because a wrong answer no longer sits near the estimate. An un-regrouped answer like 3 7/5 has the correct value (it equals 4 2/5), so an estimate cannot catch it; the separate proper-fraction check does that job.

activities.title: Study a worked carry and a worked borrow
feedback: If you cannot say where the extra sixths came from, trace them back to the one whole you broke apart: 1 = 6/6.
A worked example shows the steps but does not let you trigger the exchange on your own numbers — pair it with hands-on or written practice on fresh problems.
Matching mixed numbers to improper forms checks recognition; it does not by itself show you producing every regrouping step, so follow it with a problem you solve in full.
activities.rationale: A worked carry-and-borrow pair with revealable steps supports meaning-making; it is a scaffold, not independent practice, because the learner does not initiate the regroup on their own numbers.
learnerActions: Read a worked addition showing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 with the step 7/5 revealed as 1 + 2/5, and explain in your own words why the whole-number part becomes 4.
Read a worked subtraction showing 4 rewritten as 3 + 6/6, and answer: why change the 4 into 3 and 6 more sixths?
Match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 4 2/6 ↔ 26/6).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and explaining the regroup steps consolidates the meaning behind the exchange, even without acting it out yourself.

constraints: Lock the denominator as a fixed unit so fifths add to fifths; this blocks the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits.
Always check whether fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup so answers are proper mixed numbers (7/5 → 1 2/5).

Worked-example or revealable-step formats support meaning but do not let the learner trigger the exchange on their own numbers — treat them as scaffolds and follow with independent construction on fresh problems.

Recognition and matching tasks (mixed-to-improper, choosing the right answer) can check understanding but do not elicit the learner's own step-by-step regrouping; include tasks where the learner shows every step.
Teach both methods; do not present the improper route as the only correct one — the separate-parts route is where the borrow and carry become meaningful.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 4 2/5; 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2 (improper: 26/6 − 11/6 = 15/6 = 2 1/2); 2 3/5 = 13/5. The subtraction's fraction parts give 2/6 − 5/6 = −3/6 = −1/2, so the answer sits about half a whole below the whole-number estimate of 3 (hence around 2 1/2). All consistent. The wrong answers 3 3/6, 3 7/5 and 7/10 appear only as errors to diagnose, never as valid options.

The original quiz design listed answer choices 2 1/2 and 2 3/6 together, which are equal (both correct); this ambiguous multiple-choice set was not reproduced as a learner question — only the genuine distractor 3 3/6 is used, as an error to diagnose.

The original source claimed the topic is 'planar' so '3D adds nothing' and that 'talk cannot enact the borrow'; these are catalog-format judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than asserted. Spoken explanation and physical fraction pieces can both support this learning; no comparative necessity is claimed here.
The number-line representation from the original is included as an optional alternative view in the first activity.

probeDeeper: In the subtraction, why did you turn the 4 into a 3 — where did the extra sixths come from?
Estimate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 before finishing — should it be above or below 4? How do you know?
Could you do the subtraction by turning both into improper fractions instead? Try it and see if you get the same.
Is 3 7/5 a tidy way to leave a mixed number — why or why not?

errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fraction part of the sum has a changed denominator (7/10 rather than 7/5); the whole numbers may be added correctly

responseLevels.gap: Adds across the fraction parts, or never borrows (3 3/6); the denominator is not held as a fixed unit and regrouping is absent.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing every step: first 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, then 4 2/6 − 1 5/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items are engineered to force the two signature moves: the sum crosses a whole (fraction parts 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5), so a child who does not regroup leaves 3 7/5; the subtraction needs a borrow (2/6 < 5/6), so a child who subtracts column-by-column takes |2−5| and lands on 3 3/6. Watching the METHOD — not just the answer — reveals which happened, and the add-across error shows up immediately as a changed denominator. A child who regroups both ways, or who converts to improper fractions and gets 4 2/5 and 2 1/2, has the idea; the specific wrong answer names the specific fault.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 1/3 and 1/6, can they find a common denominator and work out the total — showing their working?

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting fractions whose denominators are RELATED — one is a multiple of the other (1/3 + 1/6, 3/4 − 1/8, 2/5 + 3/10). The pivotal new idea is that unlike parts cannot be combined until they are the SAME size: you must rename one fraction as an equivalent fraction so both share a common unit (a common denominator), then count like parts as before. Because the denominators are related, only ONE fraction needs converting (1/3 = 2/6), which makes this the gentle bridge from same-denominator work to fully unlike denominators. The equivalence must scale numerator and denominator together — the heart of getting it right.
bestPractices: Establish the NEED for a common unit first (you can't add thirds and sixths as they are) using a representation that makes different-sized parts obvious, before any rule.
Exploit the related structure: spot that the larger denominator is already the common one, so only one fraction is renamed.
Insist that renaming scales BOTH numerator and denominator (1/3 → 2/6, not 1/6) — the commonest slip is changing only the denominator.
Use estimation to judge reasonableness (1/3 + 1/6 must be more than 1/3, so 2/9 can't be right).
Simplify the result and check it against a model; connect back to counting like units once the denominators match.
Choose representations that hold the unit constant (fraction strips, number lines); avoid ones (e.g. dot paper) shown to reinforce adding without a common denominator.
keyRepresentations: Two fraction strips with related partitions (thirds and sixths) overlaid so one must be re-partitioned to match
Number line where thirds are subdivided into sixths to align the two fractions
Fraction circles/area model showing 1/3 recut into 2/6 to give a common denominator (IES Fig 6)
Equivalence chain 1/3 = 2/6 shown as cutting each third in two (numerator doubles with denominator)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9, combining numerators and denominators (NFER's 3/9-type error).
Renames the denominator without scaling the numerator: converts 1/3 to 1/6 and gets 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 — 'just inserts the larger denominator' (IES).
Forgets to simplify the result (leaves 3/6 rather than 1/2), or doesn't recognise the answer can be reduced.

learn.summary: Adding and subtracting fractions whose denominators are RELATED — one denominator is a multiple of the other (1/3 + 1/6, 3/4 − 1/8, 2/5 + 3/10). The central new idea: when you combine fractions by counting parts, the parts must be the same size, so one fraction is renamed as an equivalent fraction sharing a common unit (common denominator), after which like parts are counted as before. Because the denominators are related, only ONE fraction needs converting (e.g. 1/3 = 2/6), making this a gentle bridge from same-denominator work to fully unlike denominators. Renaming must scale numerator AND denominator together — the heart of getting it right.

activities.title: Align the strips: cut thirds into sixths to make a common unit
feedback: If a learner tries to add across (1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9): point to the strips — the pieces are different sizes, so there is nothing to count yet; the parts must be made the same size first.

If a learner changes only the denominator (1/3 → 1/6): show that cutting the one third-piece in two produces TWO sixth-pieces, not one, so the top number must double when the bottom doubles; 1/6 is visibly smaller than 1/3 on the strip.

If the sum is left as 3/6: ask 'is 3/6 finished, or can it be written with smaller numbers?' and confirm on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length. Do not reteach the adding step — it is correct.
Estimation check: 1/3 plus a bit must be MORE than 1/3, so an answer less than 1/3 (2/9 is less than 1/3, since 1/3 = 3/9) cannot be right.
activities.rationale: The need for a common unit is felt when unlike parts will not combine by counting until one is re-partitioned; a strip or number-line model can force the re-partition and show the numerator scaling as the piece is cut. Representations that hold the unit (the whole) constant — fraction strips, number lines, fraction circles — cue the need for a common denominator; dot paper has been noted in the IES guide as reinforcing adding without one. The related structure means the larger denominator is already the common unit, so only one fraction is renamed, and renaming must scale numerator and denominator together.
sourceClaims: Students often fail to convert to a common denominator and instead just insert the larger denominator; the error reflects not understanding that different denominators are different-sized unit fractions and that adding requires a common unit. Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.

On different-denominator items only 54% of Year 6 were correct; a common error was adding both numerators and denominators (2/3 + ... → 3/9); NFER recommends practising common denominators where one denominator is a multiple of the other, working visually (rectangles split into thirds and sixths).
Generating equivalent fractions by scaling numerator and denominator together (a/b = na/nb) is prerequisite to finding common denominators.
learnerActions: Try to combine 1/3 and 1/6 using a thirds strip and a sixths strip laid together; notice the pieces are different sizes and do not line up as they are.
Cut each third-piece in half so each single third becomes TWO sixth-pieces; watch the label change 1/3 → 2/6 as the one piece splits into two and the numerator ticks 1→2.
Now that every piece is a sixth, combine: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6.
Simplify 3/6 to 1/2 and check on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length.

Repeat the same cut-to-match process for 3/4 − 1/8 (recut quarters into eighths, giving 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8) and 2/5 + 3/10 (recut fifths into tenths, giving 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10), simplifying where possible.
activities.intendedInsight: When you add by counting parts, thirds and sixths must be made the same size first; cutting each third in two makes it two sixths (so the numerator doubles exactly as the denominator doubles), and only then do both fractions share one common unit and combine by counting like parts.

activities.title: Equivalence-and-combine practice that surfaces common errors
feedback: Selecting 2/9: the two denominators are not things to combine; they signal different-sized parts that must be made the same size first.
Selecting 2/6: the denominator was renamed but the numerator stayed at 1 — cutting each third in two makes TWO sixths, so the top doubles too.
If the chain is correct but left as 3/6: prompt for simplest form and confirm 3/6 = 1/2.
activities.rationale: Related-denominator sums and the equivalence step are scorable and can deliberately bait both the add-across and rename-denominator-only errors, surfacing the specific misconception for targeted feedback. A recognition/short-answer format is a useful diagnostic and practice companion; recognising a correct option is not the same as independently performing the re-partition, so it should sit alongside a task where the learner does the conversion.

Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.

On different-denominator items only 54% of Year 6 were correct; a common error was adding both numerators and denominators (2/3 + ... → 3/9); NFER recommends practising common denominators where one denominator is a multiple of the other, working visually (rectangles split into thirds and sixths).
learnerActions: Complete the chain: 1/3 = __/6, so 1/3 + 1/6 = __/6 = __ (simplest form).
Choose the correct value of 1/3 + 1/6 from options that include the correct answer, 2/9 (the add-across error) and 2/6 (denominator renamed but numerator left at 1).
Match each fraction to its equivalent written over the common denominator (e.g. 1/3 ↔ 2/6, 3/4 ↔ 6/8).
Explain in words why only one of the two fractions needed changing.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking equivalence and combining in a scorable format can reveal whether the learner renames both numerator and denominator together and whether they look for a common unit at all; it does not by itself show they can carry out the re-partition unaided.

activities.title: Read a worked conversion, then perform your own
feedback: After the worked example, ask the learner to state why the numerator doubled; if they cannot, return to cutting each part in two on a strip.
If they can read but not reproduce the conversion, give another related pair and have them do the cut themselves.
activities.rationale: A static worked conversion can present one correct renaming as a reference anchor, but on its own it does not let the learner perform the re-partition that builds the understanding; it works best paired with a task where the learner does the conversion.

Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.
learnerActions: Study a single worked conversion where 1/3 is shown recut as 2/6 over the common denominator, with the numerator and denominator both doubling.
Explain what happened to the top number and why.
Then perform the conversion yourself on a fresh related pair (e.g. rename 2/5 as tenths, giving 4/10) and complete the calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear worked example of renaming can anchor the 'scale both parts together' idea, but the learner must then carry out the re-partition themselves to secure it; reading a conversion does not by itself elicit producing one.

constraints: Establish the NEED for a common unit before any rule, using a representation that makes different-sized parts obvious (thirds and sixths cannot be counted together as they are).
Renaming must scale BOTH numerator and denominator together (1/3 → 2/6, not 1/6); the commonest slip is changing only the denominator.
Use estimation to judge reasonableness (1/3 + 1/6 must be more than 1/3, so 2/9 cannot be right).
Always simplify the result and check it against the model (3/6 → 1/2); connect back to counting like units once denominators match.

Prefer representations that hold the unit (the whole) constant — fraction strips, number lines, fraction circles. Dot paper has been noted (IES) as reinforcing adding without a common denominator, so avoid it for this objective.

Multiple-choice and fill-in items are useful for diagnosing and practising, but a recognition response does not by itself show the learner can independently perform the re-partition and combine; include a task where they carry out the conversion.

If paper fraction strips or circles are used as physical manipulatives, keep the represented whole constant and explicit each time pieces are cut, so the mathematical fraction — not the physical object — is what is combined; the slight thickness of real card is a negligible approximation of the ideal flat region it stands for.

Scope this to RELATED denominators (one a multiple of the other) so exactly one fraction is renamed; fully unlike denominators are a later step. Here the fractions are quantities being combined, so the common-unit requirement is about representing both portions on one whole — it is not a comparison of unit fractions.

probeDeeper: When you changed 1/3 into sixths, what happened to the top number, and why?
A friend writes 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9. Is 2/9 bigger or smaller than 1/3? Can adding something to 1/3 give you less than 1/3?
Why did you only need to change ONE of the two fractions here?
Is 3/6 finished, or can it be written more simply? How do you know they're the same?
assess.correctAnswer: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. 3/4 − 1/8 = 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8. Rename one fraction to the common denominator (scaling numerator and denominator together), then combine like parts and simplify.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across the unlike denominators: '1 and 1 is 2 on top, 3 and 6 is 9 on the bottom, so 2/9' — treats the two denominators as things to combine.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use strips/circles that only combine when parts match: thirds and sixths can't be added until the third is recut into sixths. Add an estimation check — 1/3 + a bit must exceed 1/3, so 2/9 (which is less than 1/3) can't be right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2/9 (or 2/12 for the second, combining 4 and 8); no common denominator is sought.

errorPatterns.pattern: Renames the denominator but not the numerator: '1/3 becomes 1/6, so 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6' — just inserts the larger denominator.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the equivalence on a model: cutting each third in two makes the one piece become TWO sixth-pieces, so 1/3 = 2/6 — the top must double when the bottom doubles. Contrast 1/6 (too small) against 1/3 on the strip.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 1/3 to 1/6 (numerator unchanged); the equivalent fraction is wrong before adding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines correctly but leaves the answer unsimplified: writes 3/6 (or doesn't reduce), not recognising 1/2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach adding — it's correct. Prompt: 'is 3/6 finished, or can you write it with smaller numbers?' Check on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct unsimplified result (3/6); the operation is right, only the final simplest-form step is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across (2/9) or renames the denominator without scaling the numerator (2/6); no common-unit reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Renames the necessary fraction (scaling numerator and denominator together), combines the like parts, simplifies (3/6→1/2), and explains that a common unit is needed to add; transfers to a fresh related-denominator pair.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to a common denominator and combines correctly for the straightforward case, but scales inconsistently, forgets to simplify, or can't say why only one fraction was changed — procedure without the equivalence reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing each step: 1/3 + 1/6, and 3/4 − 1/8. Give each answer in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The denominators are related (6 is a multiple of 3; 8 of 4), so the child must convert exactly one fraction — revealing whether equivalence is understood. Add-across yields 2/9 / 2/12 (denominators combined), impossible if a common unit is sought. Renaming without scaling yields 2/6 (numerator left at 1). A correct solver converts 1/3→2/6 (numerator scales with denominator), combines the like parts, and simplifies. Watching the conversion step is the discriminator; the simplify step is a separate check.

sources.claim: Students often fail to convert to a common denominator and instead just insert the larger denominator; the error reflects not understanding that different denominators are different-sized unit fractions and that adding requires a common unit. pedagogy.summary: These are word problems that apply like-denominator addition and subtraction of fractions and mixed numbers in context — juice poured from a jug (separate, subtract), ribbon lengths joined (combine, add). The mathematics is already secured; the new demand is READING the situation to decide join versus separate, modelling it, computing, and interpreting the answer back in context (including regrouping a fraction sum that crosses a whole, e.g. 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4). Teach by drawing the story on a bar or number line before writing symbols, holding the denominator as a fixed unit, and estimating with whole numbers to sanity-check.
bestPractices: Model the story on a bar/number line before writing the equation — draw the jug emptying or the ribbons joining
Decide join (+) vs separate (−) from the situation, and say which quantity is being removed or combined
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit (eighths stay eighths) to block add-across
Estimate with whole numbers first, then check the exact answer against it
Interpret the result in context and regroup a crossing sum (8/8 → 1 whole)

Number line for combining/removing lengths

learn.summary: Learners apply like-denominator addition and subtraction of fractions and mixed numbers to word problems (juice poured from a jug = separate/subtract; ribbons joined end to end = combine/add). The computation is already secured; the new demand is READING the situation to choose join versus separate, drawing a matching model, computing with the denominator held as a fixed unit, regrouping a fraction sum that crosses a whole (e.g. 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4), and interpreting the result back in context. Core approach: draw the story on a bar or number line before writing symbols, keep eighths as eighths to block adding across, and estimate with whole numbers to sanity-check.

activities.title: Model the story before you compute
feedback: If a learner adds across (2 3/8 + 1 5/8 → 3 8/16), re-anchor eighths as a fixed unit on the bar: three eighths and five eighths is eight eighths. The denominator counts the size of the pieces and does not change when you combine them.

If a learner picks the wrong operation (answers 5/4 for the jug, or subtracts the ribbons), draw the action first — juice leaving the jug, or ribbons laid together — and name 'take away' or 'combine' before writing the symbol.
If a learner reports 3 8/8 for the ribbons, prompt 'how much is 8/8? then add it to the whole part' — the addition was correct and only needs tidying into 4.
Estimate first: the ribbons are about 2 + 2 = 4 inches, so a 3-something answer is a warning sign.
activities.rationale: Adding across denominators is the central documented error in fraction addition/subtraction, and visual models that hold the unit constant with 'which is bigger / more or fewer than you started' reasoning support correct joining and separating. Drawing the story before symbolising, and estimating with whole numbers, targets operation-choice and the crossing-sum regroup directly.

Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: Read: 'A jug holds 3/4 of a litre of juice; 2/4 of a litre is poured out — how much is left?' Draw a bar showing 3/4, shade the 2/4 poured away, and read the remaining 1/4 off your picture.
Read: 'Two ribbons are 2 3/8 inches and 1 5/8 inches long — what is their total length?' Draw the two ribbons laid end to end on a bar marked in eighths.
Before writing any symbols, say aloud whether the story is a 'take away' or a 'combine', and name which quantity is removed or joined.
Write the matching equation, keeping the denominator fixed (quarters stay quarters, eighths stay eighths): 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4; 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 4.
When the fraction parts reach 8/8, regroup that whole into the whole-number count so the total reads 4 inches, not 3 8/8.
activities.intendedInsight: The story tells you the operation; a picture drawn first makes join-versus-separate visible, and holding the denominator as a fixed unit means combining 3/8 and 5/8 gives 8/8 = one whole, never 8/16.

activities.title: Act out pouring and joining with a locked-unit model
feedback: If the learner expects 3-something for the ribbons, point to the moment 8/8 fuses into a whole: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4. 3 8/16 is wrong, while 3 8/8 has the right value but should be regrouped as 4.
If the learner is unsure which operation a story needs, use the 'more or fewer than you started?' check: pouring out leaves fewer, joining makes more.
activities.rationale: Choosing the operation and modelling the story is the target skill, and an interactive surface where units stay locked lets a learner act out pouring/joining and see the equation update. Note: an interactive model is proposed as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible; a drawn bar or number line can achieve the same modelling without the live surface, so the medium is not uniquely required.
sourceClaims: The add-across misconception is the central documented error in fraction addition/subtraction; visual fraction models that hold the unit constant and 'which is bigger' reasoning support correct joining/separating
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: In a story workspace, pick the jug context and pour 2/4 out of a 3/4-litre jug; watch the removed part grey out, leaving 1/4, and read 'take away' straight off the picture.
Switch to the ribbon context and drag two ribbons (marked in eighths) end to end; watch the eighths auto-count as they join.
Notice that when 3/8 and 5/8 meet at 8/8 the eighths fuse into one whole inch and the total snaps to 4 inches.
Read the matching ± equation that the picture produces, and use a 'more or fewer than you started with?' check to confirm the direction of the operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Combining the fraction parts can make a whole appear in the whole-number count (8/8 → 1 whole), and when the pieces are kept as fixed eighths, adding across into sixteenths is not even a possible move.

activities.title: Study then classify the two story structures
feedback: If a story is misclassified, re-read for the action and what is unknown: words like 'poured out', 'left', 'remains' often go with separating and 'total', 'altogether', 'joined' often go with combining, but check the situation rather than relying on the word (e.g. '1/4 L was left after 2/4 L was poured out; how much was there at first?' needs addition).
If a matched equation changes the denominator (e.g. 8/16), flag it: the piece size stays the same when like fractions are combined.

Sorting and matching check whether the operation choice is secure, but do not by themselves elicit independent drawing of a new story; follow with drawing or modelling a fresh story so the learner also builds the reading, not only recognises it.
activities.rationale: Operation-choice and the add-across/unregrouped errors are cleanly surfaced by distractors built from those exact mistakes. Recognition and sorting tasks can diagnose the choice efficiently, but they do not by themselves elicit independent reading-and-modelling of a new story, so pair them with construction.
sourceClaims: Same-denominator addition is answered correctly by the large majority of pupils, but a minority add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and estimation aid remediation
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: Study a worked pour-out (jug: 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4) and a worked join (ribbons: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4), revealing the shaded/combined model and then the answer for each.
Answer 'what does 8/8 make?' for the ribbon total and explain where that whole goes in the answer.
Sort a set of new stories into 'combine' versus 'take away', then match each story to the ± equation that solves it.
Fill in a missing answer that requires a regroup step, and explain the regroup in words.
activities.intendedInsight: Pour-out stories separate (subtract) and joining stories combine (add); naming the structure first makes the correct operation and any crossing-sum regroup predictable.

activities.title: Talk through pour and join stories with a context character
feedback: If the learner names the wrong operation, slow down on the action word and run the 'more or fewer?' check before touching any number.
When the talk reaches 8/8, ask the learner to draw or point to where that whole joins the whole-number count (giving 4), since the conversation alone does not show the regroup happening.
activities.rationale: An in-role character can pose and vary stories and probe direction, which is proposed as one way to rehearse the reading of join versus separate. No cited source establishes the efficacy of the conversational medium itself; the source support attaches to the paired drawn bar/number line and estimation the activity pairs with. Its observable limit is that a conversation does not supply a visual surface where fraction parts combine, so it is paired with a drawn model; this is not evidence that dialogue is required or superior.
sourceClaims: Same-denominator addition is answered correctly by the large majority of pupils, but a minority add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and estimation aid remediation
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: An in-role kitchen/craft character poses a pour-out story and a join story and varies the numbers; before any calculation, restate whether each story is 'take away' or 'combine' and name which quantity is removed or joined.
Answer the character's 'more or fewer than you started?' probe for each story to confirm the operation direction.

Explain your reasoning aloud; where the fraction parts need to be seen combining (e.g. 3/8 + 5/8 reaching 8/8), draw a bar or number line alongside the talk and point to where the whole joins the whole-number count (→ 4).
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through a story and naming its structure can rehearse operation-choice and direction, but a spoken exchange does not itself display the fraction parts fusing, so it is paired with a drawn model when the crossing-sum regroup needs to be seen.

constraints: All fractions in a problem must refer to the same whole and share a like denominator; these tasks do not cover unlike-denominator addition.
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit: combining 3/8 and 5/8 gives 8/8 = 1 whole, never 8/16. The denominator names the piece size and does not change when like fractions are joined.
Regroup any crossing sum: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 4; 3 8/8 has the same value but has not been regrouped, so write the final answer as 4.

Sorting, matching and multiple-choice tasks assess operation-choice but do not elicit independent drawing/modelling of a new story; use construction tasks (draw the model, write and solve the equation) to build that skill.
A tap-to-reveal worked pair illustrates the two structures but does not let a learner model a fresh story — treat it as a scaffold, then move to learner-constructed models.

An interactive locked-unit model, a hand-drawn bar/number line, and an in-role conversation can each support the reading/modelling in different ways; none is uniquely necessary, so do not require a particular medium.
