topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 7/8 of a chocolate bar and gives away 3/8, can they work out what fraction is left — and then show two different ways to split 7/8 into two parts?

pedagogy.summary: The conceptual glue beneath fraction operations: understanding addition and subtraction as JOINING and SEPARATING like parts, and being able to DECOMPOSE a fraction into a sum of same-denominator parts in more than one way (3/8 = 1/8+1/8+1/8 and also 1/8+2/8; 2 1/8 = 1+1+1/8). It moves a child from 'apply the numerator rule' to 'a fraction is a flexible collection of unit parts I can split and recombine however I like'. This flexibility is what makes later work — mixed-number arithmetic, common denominators, regrouping in subtraction — make sense rather than being separate tricks.
bestPractices: Frame + and − explicitly as joining and separating the SAME unit parts, keeping the denominator (the unit) fixed throughout.
Demand MORE THAN ONE decomposition of the same fraction so flexibility, not a single memorised split, is the goal (5/6 = 1/6+4/6 = 2/6+3/6 = ...).
Connect decomposition to the whole: 2 1/8 is two whole sets of eighths plus one eighth (16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8), so mixed numbers are seen as one quantity of like parts.
Justify each decomposition on a visual model (bar/number line) where the total length is invariant — different sums, same measure.
Use decomposition to explain, not just compute: e.g. why 5/6 − 2/6 separates two sixths from five.
keyRepresentations: Fraction bar that can be sliced into groups in multiple ways, total length fixed
Number line showing a fraction reached by different combinations of unit-fraction jumps
Part-part-whole / bar model linking a fraction to its decompositions
Mixed-number bar showing whole sets of the unit plus the extra part (2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8)
commonMisconceptions: Alters denominators when decomposing (a reverse add-across): writes 5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6, so the parts don't actually total 5/6.
Believes a fraction has only one 'correct' break-up (3/8 must be 1/8+1/8+1/8) and cannot produce a different valid decomposition.
Treats a mixed number's whole and fraction parts as disconnected numbers, unable to express 2 1/8 as a single count of eighths (17/8).

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 learn to see fraction addition and subtraction as JOINING and SEPARATING the same unit parts, with the denominator (the unit) held fixed throughout. The central skill is decomposing a fraction into a sum of same-denominator parts in MORE THAN ONE way (5/6 = 1/6+4/6 = 2/6+3/6 = 1/6+1/6+3/6), and expressing a mixed number as a single count of like parts (2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8 = 17/8). The aim is to shift from 'apply the numerator rule' to 'a fraction is a flexible collection of unit parts I can split and recombine', which later makes mixed-number arithmetic, common denominators, and regrouping in subtraction coherent rather than separate tricks.

activities.title: Slice one bar many ways
feedback: When several different sums all align with the same bar length, point out explicitly: different sums, same measure — that is what makes 5/6 flexible.

If a learner relabels a piece's denominator wrongly (e.g. calls a two-sixths piece '2/3'), rebuild that piece from sixth-sized units on the bar and recount: it is 2/6. A two-sixths piece does equal 1/3, but this task asks for same-denominator sums, so record every part in sixths.
If a learner can give only one break-up, prompt: 'Find a genuinely different way, then another' until two or more distinct valid sums appear.
Optional live interaction, where available: let cuts on the bar auto-write the matching sum and refuse any attempt to relabel a piece's denominator, so the reverse add-across cannot be recorded.
activities.rationale: Decomposition is literally slicing one fixed quantity into groups in different ways. A model whose total length is invariant lets a child generate many decompositions, see they all measure the same, and keeps attention on the unit. Understanding why procedures work by composing/decomposing into like units is what prevents treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers.
sourceClaims: Fraction computation errors stem from not treating the fraction as a single number and operating on numerators and denominators as separate whole numbers; understanding why procedures work (composition/decomposition into like units) prevents this.
Decomposing a non-unit fraction into unit fractions and multiple same-denominator sums, via dual naming, builds the flexible joining/separating that underpins mixed-number arithmetic.
learnerActions: Start with a bar whose total length represents 5/6 of a whole, marked off into five equal sixths (each one-sixth of the whole) against a fixed ruler so its length cannot change.
Group the sixths one way (e.g. 1 and 4) and write the matching sum of sixths underneath: 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6.
Regroup the SAME bar differently (2 and 3; then 1, 1 and 3) and write each new sum: 2/6 + 3/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 3/6.
Line up all the sums you have written against the single unchanged bar and say aloud: 'all of these are 5/6'.
Repeat the whole process with a fresh fraction you have not seen (e.g. 7/8) to produce at least two distinct decompositions.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction is not one fixed break-up: any grouping of its unit parts that uses the same denominator and the same total count measures the same quantity. Addition joins those parts and subtraction separates them, while the unit stays fixed.

activities.title: Mixed number as one count of like parts
feedback: If a learner writes 2 1/8 as 2/8 + 1/8, show each whole bar as 8/8 on the model and recount: two wholes are 16/8, so 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8.
If the '2' is ignored, ask first 'How many eighths are in one whole? in two wholes?' before writing the conversion.
Reinforce by reversing it: start from 17/8 and build back the two whole eighths-bars plus one eighth.
activities.rationale: Treating a mixed number's whole and fraction as disconnected numbers blocks mixed-number arithmetic. Building the wholes out of the same unit on a model makes the conversion a count, not a memorised rule.
sourceClaims: Decomposing a non-unit fraction into unit fractions and multiple same-denominator sums, via dual naming, builds the flexible joining/separating that underpins mixed-number arithmetic.
learnerActions: Lay out 2 1/8 as two whole bars, each cut into eight eighths, plus one extra eighth.
Count the eighths in each whole bar (8/8 and 8/8), then join the extra eighth.
Write the quantity as a single count of eighths: 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8, confirming the 2 wholes contribute 16/8, not 2/8.
State in words why the whole and the fraction are one quantity: 2 1/8 is seventeen eighths altogether.
activities.intendedInsight: A mixed number's whole part and fraction part are the same kind of unit part; the wholes can be recounted as eighths so the whole quantity is a single count of like parts (17/8).

activities.title: Check and sort candidate decompositions
feedback: For a learner who accepts 2/3+3/3: compute 2/3+3/3 (= 5/3, more than a whole) and compare to 5/6 — it is clearly not equal, and the pieces are not sixths.
Correct answer reference: 5/6 = any two distinct sums of sixths totalling 5/6 (e.g. 1/6+4/6 and 2/6+3/6); 2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8 = 17/8; the denominator stays fixed throughout.
Recognising a correct option is a check on reasoning; it does not by itself show the learner can build one, so always pair it with the learner producing their own second decomposition.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing valid from invalid decompositions surfaces the reverse-add-across misconception, and requiring the learner to add the parts and compare keeps the focus on the fraction as a single quantity. The add-across error is a documented, common mistake among primary pupils.
sourceClaims: The add-across (adding numerators and denominators) error is a common, documented mistake among primary pupils, evidencing that fractions are being treated as pairs of whole numbers rather than single quantities.

Fraction computation errors stem from not treating the fraction as a single number and operating on numerators and denominators as separate whole numbers; understanding why procedures work (composition/decomposition into like units) prevents this.
learnerActions: Given several candidate sums for 5/6, decide which equal 5/6 and which do not — e.g. 1/6+4/6, 2/6+3/6, and the trap 2/3+3/3.
For each candidate, add the parts and compare the total to 5/6 to justify the decision, not just guess.
Explain why 2/3 + 3/3 fails: adding them gives 5/3 (more than a whole), not 5/6, and the parts are not measured in sixths.
Fill in a second valid decomposition of a given fraction, and match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 2 1/8 ↔ 17/8).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid same-denominator decomposition must keep the denominator fixed AND have parts that actually total the original fraction; the reverse add-across (2/3+3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6) produces parts that do not sum to 5/6.

activities.title: Explain, don't just compute, subtraction as separating
feedback: If a learner changes the denominator during subtraction, re-anchor on the unit: both numbers are sixths, so the answer is counted in sixths.
Ask the learner to verify by re-joining the result to the amount removed and checking they return to 5/6.
activities.rationale: Using decomposition to explain rather than only compute builds the conceptual glue that makes regrouping in subtraction sensible later. Holding the unit fixed prevents treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers.
sourceClaims: Fraction computation errors stem from not treating the fraction as a single number and operating on numerators and denominators as separate whole numbers; understanding why procedures work (composition/decomposition into like units) prevents this.
learnerActions: Show 5/6 − 2/6 on a bar or number line by separating two sixths from five sixths and reading the remaining three sixths.
Say in words what subtraction did: it separated two of the same unit parts, leaving 3/6; the denominator (sixths) did not change.
Connect it to joining: 3/6 + 2/6 rebuilds the original 5/6, so joining and separating are opposite moves on the same unit parts.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction separates like unit parts just as addition joins them; the denominator names the unit and stays fixed, so only the count of parts changes.

constraints: Keep the denominator (the unit) fixed throughout every join, separate, and decomposition; this is the non-negotiable idea that blocks the reverse add-across.
Always demand MORE THAN ONE decomposition of the same fraction; a single memorised split does not demonstrate flexibility.

The reverse add-across (5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3) is a genuine error, not an acceptable alternative answer: its parts sum to 5/3, not 5/6, and are not measured in sixths. Never present it as valid; use it only as a checked-and-rejected trap.
2 wholes of eighths are 16/8, not 2/8; ensure the whole part is recounted in the shared unit before converting (2 1/8 = 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8).

Selecting or recognising a correct decomposition is a check on reasoning and does not by itself show independent construction; pair recognition tasks with the learner producing their own decompositions.
Static worked examples can show a couple of decompositions for reference but cannot let the child generate new groupings, which is the actual skill; treat them as support, not the main activity.
Justify each decomposition against a model where the total measure is invariant (fixed-length bar or number line), so different sums are seen to share one measure.

Narrow medium affordances (not universal laws): discussion alone can support explaining a decomposition but does not itself let a child perform the slicing and grouping; and because this content is planar part-whole reasoning, a 3D/spatial model adds no dimension the task needs. Neither observation means any medium 'cannot teach' — explaining aloud is retained as part of several activities.

Self-audit: confirmed 2 1/8 = 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8 (two wholes contribute 16/8, not 2/8). Confirmed 2/3 + 3/3 = 5/3 ≠ 5/6, so it is correctly treated as an invalid decomposition rather than an alternative answer. Confirmed example decompositions of 5/6 (1/6+4/6, 2/6+3/6, 1/6+1/6+3/6) and of 7/8 each total the named fraction.

The source's categorical dismissals of 3D and conversation were reworded into narrow affordances rather than carried as universal pedagogical laws.

probeDeeper: You wrote 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6 — can you find a different way? And another after that?
A friend says 5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3. Add 2/3 and 3/3 and check — does it come to 5/6?
How many eighths are in the two whole ones of 2 1/8? So how many eighths altogether?
If addition is joining parts, what is subtraction doing — show 5/6 − 2/6 as separating.
assess.correctAnswer: 5/6 = e.g. 1/6 + 4/6 AND 2/6 + 3/6 (any two distinct sums of sixths totalling 5/6). 2 1/8 = 1 + 1 + 1/8 = 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8. Denominator stays sixths/eighths throughout.

errorPatterns.pattern: Alters the denominators when decomposing: '5/6 is 2/3 + 3/3 because 2 and 3 make 5, and 3 and 3 make 6' — a reverse add-across, so the parts don't total 5/6.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to unit-fraction building blocks: 5/6 is five one-sixths, so every piece of it must be measured in sixths; rebuild the sum from sixth-pieces on a bar and check the total length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers a 'decomposition' whose pieces don't share the denominator 6 (2/3+3/3, 1/2+2/4); checking the sum gives the wrong total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a mixed number's whole and fraction as unrelated: writes 2 1/8 as '2/8 + 1/8' or can't count the wholes in eighths, so never reaches 17/8.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the two whole bars each as 8/8 on the model, then join the extra 1/8: 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8; count the whole-groups of eight before writing the numeric conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot express 2 1/8 as a single count of eighths; the '2' is ignored or mis-scaled (2/8 instead of 16/8).

responseLevels.gap: Alters denominators when decomposing (reverse add-across); can give at most one break-up; treats a mixed number's whole and fraction as unrelated numbers.
responseLevels.full: Gives two distinct sixth-decompositions of 5/6 keeping the denominator fixed, expresses 2 1/8 as a sum crossing the whole (1+1+1/8, or 17/8), and explains + and − as flexible joining/separating of like parts; transfers to a new fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Produces valid same-denominator decompositions and one way for 5/6, but struggles to find a genuinely different SECOND way, or can't link 2 1/8 to its total in eighths — can join but not yet flexibly, or can't cross the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me TWO different ways to break 5/6 into a sum of sixths. Then take 2 1/8 and write it as a sum that includes its whole parts — show it however helps you (a picture, a number line, or numbers).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for TWO decompositions forces flexible joining rather than one memorised split, and exposes the child who can only give a single break-up. A child who alters denominators (5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3) reveals the reverse add-across — valid sixths must keep the denominator 6. The 2 1/8 task reveals whether the whole and the fraction are seen as one quantity of eighths (17/8) or two disconnected numbers. Watching the moves shows whether the unit is held fixed while the counts are recombined.

Subtract 1 3/5 from 3 1/4 using a common denominator

pedagogy.summary: The general case: adding and subtracting fractions with UNLIKE denominators where neither is a multiple of the other (2/3 + 5/4), and mixed numbers (3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must now be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — scaling BOTH numerators, then combining like parts. Mixed numbers add a further demand: in subtraction the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrowing a whole, or converting to improper fractions). It is the culmination of the whole add/subtract strand: the same 'make the units the same, then count' idea, now with no shortcuts.
bestPractices: Reinforce that BOTH fractions must be renamed to a common unit; a common multiple of the denominators (often the product, sometimes the LCM) gives it.
Insist both numerators scale with their denominators (2/3 → 8/12, 5/4 → 15/12) — the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling slips appear.
For mixed numbers, teach two secure routes and let pupils choose: regroup/borrow a whole, OR convert to improper fractions first (often cleaner when a borrow is needed).
Use estimation and benchmarks to gate the answer (2/3 + 5/4 is more than 2, so 7/7 = 1 is impossible).
Verify with a visual model or number line, per the topic's own evidence; simplify and write mixed-number answers.
Keep units constant in representations; avoid manipulatives that encourage adding without a common denominator.
keyRepresentations: Two strips/number lines re-gridded to a common denominator (thirds and quarters → twelfths)
Area/fraction-circle model showing both fractions recut to the shared unit
Mixed-number bars showing a whole tile broken into the common unit to enable borrowing (1 whole → 20/20)
Improper-fraction conversion as an alternative route (3 1/4 = 13/4) laid beside the mixed form
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7, combining numerators and denominators.
Finds a common denominator but scales only one (or neither) numerator, or uses a wrong common denominator (2/3 = 2/12).

In mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of position (does 12/20 − 5/20), never regrouping across the whole when the minuend's fraction part is smaller.

learn.summary: General case of adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators where neither denominator is a multiple of the other (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4), extended to mixed numbers (e.g. 3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — which scales BOTH numerators, then like parts are combined. Mixed-number subtraction adds a further demand: the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrow a whole) or a conversion to improper fractions. The unifying idea remains 'make the units the same, then count', now with no shortcuts.

activities.title: Shared-grid combiner: rename both fractions, then combine
feedback: If a learner writes 7/7 (adding tops and adding bottoms), re-partition both fractions on the strips and estimate first: 5/4 alone exceeds 1, so 2/3 + 5/4 must exceed 1, and 7/7 = 1 cannot be right.

If a learner finds the common denominator but leaves a numerator unscaled (e.g. writes 2/12 for 2/3), rebuild the equivalence on the model — one third cut into twelfths becomes FOUR twelfths, so 2/3 = 8/12 — and have them check both conversions before combining.
If the sum is left as 23/12, prompt converting to a mixed number and simplifying: 23/12 = 1 11/12.
Confirm with the estimate: 23/12 is more than 1 and a little less than 2, matching 'more than one (5/4) plus two-thirds'.
activities.rationale: Adding or subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions over a common unit; the add-across error and the 'use the larger denominator' error both come from not grasping this, and a chosen pair where neither denominator is a multiple of the other forces both numerators to scale, exposing partial-scaling slips. Estimation and benchmarks let learners judge reasonableness. A dynamic re-gridding model (strips that only align once a shared grid is chosen, with both numerators re-scaling as the grid is set) may make the re-unitising visible, but a fully worked static picture of 2/3 and 5/4 both shown as twelfths can also anchor the equivalence.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.
The add-across error on different-denominator items is made mostly by lower- and middle-achieving pupils and remains common; visual work and staged conversion help.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Set up 2/3 + 5/4 on two strips or two number lines, one gridded in thirds and one in quarters, and notice they will not combine while the units differ.
Choose a shared unit (a common multiple of 3 and 4) and re-grid both strips into twelfths, re-tiling each fraction: 2/3 becomes 8/12 and 5/4 becomes 15/12.

State explicitly that cutting each third into four pieces turns 2/3 into 8/12 — the top is multiplied by the same factor as the bottom — and check the same for 5/4 (each quarter cut into three, so 5/4 = 15/12) before combining.
Combine the re-tiled pieces to get 23/12 and regroup into the mixed number 1 11/12.

Before computing, estimate: 5/4 is already more than 1, so adding a positive 2/3 makes the sum more than 1 (indeed more than 1.5). That already rules out answers like 7/7 = 1; the true sum lands just below 2 (23/12, just under 24/12).
activities.intendedInsight: Unlike fractions can only be combined once BOTH are rewritten over the same unit; each numerator scales by the same factor as its own denominator, and estimation gates whether a result is even possible.

activities.title: Mixed-number subtraction with a regroup across the whole
feedback: If a learner subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger regardless of position (e.g. does 12/20 − 5/20 and writes 7/20), model breaking one whole of the 3 into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract; or convert both to improper fractions (65/20 − 32/20) to avoid the borrow.
If a learner is stuck because '5/20 minus 12/20 can't be done', show that the whole provides the extra twentieths: 2 25/20 − 1 12/20 = 1 13/20.
Check that the final answer is written as a simplified mixed number where appropriate.
Verify with the improper-fraction route: 65/20 − 32/20 = 33/20 = 1 13/20, matching the regroup route.
activities.rationale: Mixed-number subtraction where the fraction part becomes smaller after conversion forces a regroup across the whole; offering two secure routes — borrowing a whole, or converting to improper fractions — lets learners choose and builds understanding of why the borrow is needed. A bar model in which a whole tile breaks into the common unit can make the borrow concrete; the improper-fraction conversion laid beside the mixed form shows an equivalent clean alternative. This targets the common error of subtracting smaller-from-larger in each column without regrouping.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Set up 3 1/4 − 1 3/5 and rename both fractions to a common denominator of twentieths: 3 5/20 − 1 12/20.
Notice that 5/20 is smaller than 12/20, so the fraction part cannot be taken directly — a regroup across the whole is needed.
Regroup one whole from the 3 into twentieths: break a whole tile into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract to get 1 13/20.
As an alternative route, convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions first (3 1/4 = 13/4 = 65/20 and 1 3/5 = 8/5 = 32/20), subtract to 33/20, and convert back to 1 13/20.
Compare the two routes and decide which you find cleaner when a borrow is needed.
activities.intendedInsight: When the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller than the subtrahend's after finding a common denominator, you must regroup a whole into the common unit (or work with improper fractions) rather than subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger in each column.

activities.title: Explain and check with a model
feedback: Full understanding: renames both fractions to a real common denominator (scaling both numerators), combines, handles the mixed-number regroup, simplifies to a mixed-number answer, verifies with a model, and transfers to a new unlike-denominator pair including mixed numbers.

Partial understanding: finds a correct common denominator and adds unlike proper fractions reliably (23/12), but the mixed-number subtraction breaks down when a regroup is needed, or answers aren't simplified/converted — the procedure holds for the easy case but not the borrow.
Gap: adds across (7/7) or scales only one/neither numerator; in the mixed subtraction subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never regroups.
activities.rationale: A performance task in which neither denominator is a multiple of the other, and the mixed subtraction is built so the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller after conversion, discriminates whether equivalence, common-multiple choice, and regrouping are all in place. Asking learners to explain their choice of denominator and to test an absurd result against an estimate surfaces reasoning, not just answers.

Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 + 5/4 and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5, showing every step and giving each answer in simplest form as a mixed number where appropriate.
Explain how you chose the common denominator and why BOTH numerators changed when you did.
Answer the challenge: a friend says 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7 = 1 — but 5/4 on its own is more than 1, so can the total be exactly 1? Explain what went wrong.
For the subtraction, after reaching 3 5/20 − 1 12/20, explain what you do because you can't take 12/20 from 5/20 as it stands.
Verify 23/12 against the benchmark: confirm it is more than 1 (since 5/4 alone exceeds 1) and a little less than 2 — does that match adding 2/3 and 5/4?
activities.intendedInsight: A learner secure in this strand can rename both fractions to a genuine common denominator, handle a mixed-number regroup by either route, simplify, and verify a result against a benchmark estimate — not just execute steps.

constraints: Target age approximately 10–11 (Year 6); learners should already be able to generate equivalent fractions and convert between mixed and improper forms, since these are the enabling moves for the regroup.
A common multiple of the denominators gives the shared unit; the product always works and the least common multiple is sometimes tidier — do not teach that one specific denominator is required.
Both numerators must scale with their own denominators; the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling errors appear, so check both equivalences before combining.
Keep the unit constant within any representation and avoid manipulatives that let learners combine pieces without first establishing a common denominator.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-blank items (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4 with 7/7 as a distractor, or a mixed subtraction with the no-borrow answer as a distractor) can diagnose add-across, partial-scaling, and no-borrow errors, but recognising a correct option does not demonstrate independent construction of the renaming and regrouping; use alongside tasks where the learner carries out the full procedure.
A fully worked static picture can anchor one conversion or borrow but does not let the learner perform the re-gridding themselves; use it as a reference rather than the main activity.
Teach both the borrow-a-whole and convert-to-improper routes and let learners choose; the improper route is often cleaner precisely when a borrow would be needed.
Estimation benchmarks must be stated correctly: 2/3 + 5/4 is more than 1 (5/4 alone exceeds 1) and lands just below 2 (23/12); do not state it exceeds 2.

pedagogy.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number, understood as repeated addition of a unit fraction: a/b is a multiple of 1/b, so 5 × 1/4 is five quarters (5/4) and n × a/b = (n×a)/b. The whole number multiplies the COUNT of unit parts while the denominator — the size of the part — stays fixed. This is the first fraction multiplication and the bridge from 'a/b as a sum of 1/b' to the general product; taught on a model, 4 × 3/8 is simply four lots of three-eighths = twelve eighths.
bestPractices: Build from repeated addition: 4 × 3/8 = 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so the numerators accumulate and the eighth stays the unit.
State the rule as scaling the count only: n × a/b = (n×a)/b, with the denominator unchanged because the unit doesn't change.
Use number lines and bars where n jumps of a/b land past one whole, then re-group into a mixed number (5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4).
For a mixed number × whole, multiply EVERY part (2 1/3 × 3 = three 2s and three thirds = 6 + 3/3 = 7), ideally via the improper form 7/3 × 3.
Contrast with addition of fractions so children don't blur the two procedures.
keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated equal jumps of the unit/non-unit fraction
Fraction bars showing n copies of a/b combined
Repeated-addition equation aligned with the (n×a)/b rule
Improper↔mixed conversion of the product (6/5 = 1 1/5)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too: 4 × 3/8 = 12/32, applying the whole number to both parts instead of just the count of unit fractions.
Incompletely distributes over a mixed number: 2 1/3 × 3 = 6 1/3, multiplying the whole but forgetting the fraction part.
Confuses the operation with addition (adds 4 + 3/8) or cannot see 5 × 1/4 as five quarters.

learn.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number as repeated addition of a unit fraction: a/b is a multiple of 1/b, so 5 × 1/4 is five quarters (5/4), and n × a/b = (n×a)/b. The whole number scales the COUNT of unit parts while the denominator — the size of each part — stays fixed. For a mixed number × whole, every part is multiplied (2 1/3 × 3 = three 2s and three thirds = 6 + 3/3 = 7; equivalently 7/3 × 3 = 21/3 = 7). This is the bridge from 'a/b as a sum of 1/b' to the general product.

activities.title: Jump-counter number line for n × a/b
feedback: If a learner expects the denominator to change, point to the fixed jump size: the eighth is the step, so four hops of three-eighths are still measured in eighths — only how many eighths grows.
If four 3/8 hops are read as landing before one whole, recount the hops aloud (3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8) and mark where 8/8 = one whole falls so the past-one total is seen.
In mixed-number mode, if only the whole part is tripled, point to the three separate thirds in the three bars: three thirds make a whole, so 2 1/3 × 3 is 7, not 6 1/3.
Prompt: 'Should four lots of 3/8 be bigger or smaller than one 3/8?' to check the answer grew.
activities.rationale: An interactive number line/bar where the learner controls the number of jumps but the jump size is locked makes the count-scales-not-the-unit idea watchable, enacting repeated addition that underlies the rule. A mixed-number mode showing copies of the whole bar makes complete distribution visible. Efficacy over other media is not established; this is a proposed design on its stated affordance.
sourceClaims: Non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4); this repeated-addition composition is the conceptual basis for multiplying a fraction by a whole number, and understanding why procedures work reduces forgetting/confusing them.
Pupils should understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiply a fraction (and mixed number) by a whole number, e.g. n × a/b, supported by visual models.
learnerActions: Set the jump size to 3/8 and dial the number of jumps to 4; watch four identical hops march along the line and land on 12/8.
Re-group the landing point into a mixed number: 12/8 = 1 4/8 (= 1 1/2).

Keep the jump size fixed and change only how many jumps there are for n × 1/4 with n = 3, 5, 8, each time reading off the total count of quarters and converting past-one results to mixed or whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4; 8 × 1/4 = 8/4 = 2).
Switch to a mixed-number mode: lay three whole 2 1/3 bars end to end so every part is tripled, and read that three 2s and three thirds make 6 + 3/3 = 7.
Say aloud what changed and what stayed the same after each build: the unit (the eighth, the third) never changed, only how many of them there were.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the unit part stays the same size, multiplying by a whole number only multiplies the COUNT of parts: n × a/b = (n×a)/b, with the denominator unchanged. A mixed number × whole requires multiplying every part.

activities.title: Build from repeated addition before stating the rule
feedback: If a learner adds the whole number to the fraction (4 + 3/8), re-read the expression as 'four lots of three-eighths' and lay out the four copies to be summed.
When converting 12/8, ask how many eighths make one whole (8) so the mixed number 1 4/8 is reasoned, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Explicitly connecting the repeated-addition form to the (n×a)/b rule, and contrasting with the additive error, targets the common error of confusing the two operations and grounds the procedure in why it works.
sourceClaims: Non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4); this repeated-addition composition is the conceptual basis for multiplying a fraction by a whole number, and understanding why procedures work reduces forgetting/confusing them.
learnerActions: Write 4 × 3/8 as 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 and add the numerators while keeping the eighth as the unit, reaching 12/8.
Contrast this with the additive slip of adding the whole number to the fraction (e.g. 4 + 3/8) and explain in words how multiplication differs from addition, so the operations are not blurred.
Convert the improper product to a mixed number (12/8 = 1 1/2; 6/5 = 1 1/5) and back, naming how many whole ones and what is left over.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication of a unit or non-unit fraction by a whole number is accumulation of equal parts; the numerators accumulate and the denominator is the unchanging unit. This is distinct from adding a whole number to a fraction.

activities.title: Targeted practice that baits the multiply-denominator error
feedback: For the 12/32 option: compute 12/32 and notice it equals 3/8 — the answer did not grow, so it cannot be four lots of 3/8.
For a 6 1/3 answer to 2 1/3 × 3: ask explicitly 'what is three lots of one-third?' (3/3 = 1 whole), then replace the single 1/3 with that whole: 6 + 1 = 7.
activities.rationale: Scorable items with a pre-identified distractor surface the two documented misconceptions and ask for justification, so the response reveals whether the unit is held fixed and every part scaled. Fixed items elicit recognition/computation and can check these errors but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the model or justify aloud.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in equations such as '4 × 3/8 = _/8 = 1 _/8', writing the missing count and the mixed number.
Choose the correct value of 4 × 3/8 from options that include 12/32 (denominator wrongly multiplied), then justify why 12/32 cannot be right.
Order n × 1/4 for n = 3, 5, 8 from smallest to largest and, where it exceeds one, state each as a mixed number or whole number (5/4 = 1 1/4; 8/4 = 2).
Work 2 1/3 × 3, showing both the part-by-part method and the improper-fraction method (7/3 × 3 = 21/3 = 7).
activities.intendedInsight: Fraction × whole and mixed × whole can be computed reliably by scaling the count and keeping the unit fixed; the multiply-denominator slip gives an answer equal to the original fraction, which therefore cannot be four lots of it — a whole-number multiple greater than one must be larger than the original.

constraints: A static worked example (e.g. tapping 5/4 to reveal five quarter-pieces) can anchor the idea but does not let the learner build and vary the jumps; use it as a reference, not the main construction activity.

Multiple-choice and fill-in items elicit recognition and computation and can bait the denominator error, but do not by themselves require independent construction of the repeated-addition model or spoken justification; pair them with build-and-explain work.
Keep the unit (denominator) genuinely fixed in any model so the learner changes only the count; the pedagogical point is lost if the part size appears to change.
For mixed numbers, ensure the model or working shows EVERY part multiplied; only tripling the whole part reproduces the incomplete-distribution error.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4 × 3/8 = 12/8 = 1 4/8 = 1 1/2 ✓; 5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4 ✓; 2 1/3 × 3 = 7 (6 + 3/3), and 7/3 × 3 = 21/3 = 7 ✓; 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5 ✓; 6/5 = 1 1/5 ✓. The distractor 12/32 reduces to 3/8 ✓ — retained only as an incorrect option to be refuted, never as a valid answer.

Note on multiples: 3/8 is trivially the 1× multiple of itself; activity[2] insight now says the slip answer cannot be FOUR lots of the original (must be larger), avoiding the false claim that a fraction cannot be a multiple of itself.

The 3D and conversation artefact ratings in the source asserted these media add nothing / cannot teach this; such comparative-necessity claims are not established by catalog ratings and have been dropped rather than restated as universal laws. A number-line/bar model was retained on its stated affordance (locked unit with variable count), not as the only possible medium.

probeDeeper: Show me 5 × 1/4 as a repeated addition — how many quarters is that altogether?
A friend says 4 × 3/8 = 12/32. Work out what 12/32 is — is it bigger than 3/8? Should four lots of 3/8 be bigger or smaller than 3/8?
In 2 1/3 × 3, did you multiply BOTH the 2 and the 1/3 by 3? What is three lots of one-third?

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the denominator as well as the numerator: '4 times 3 is 12, 4 times 8 is 32, so 12/32' — applies the whole number to both parts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to repeated addition on a number line: 4 × 3/8 is four hops of three-eighths; the eighth (the unit) never changes, only how many. Contrast 12/32 = 3/8 — the answer didn't grow, so it can't be four lots.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 12/32 (or reduces it back to 3/8); the denominator changes when it shouldn't.

errorPatterns.pattern: Incompletely distributes over the mixed number: '2 1/3 times 3 is 6 1/3' — multiplies the whole part but leaves the fraction part unmultiplied.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show three whole 2 1/3 bars: three 2s AND three thirds; or convert to 7/3 first and multiply. Emphasise every part is copied three times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer keeps the original fraction part (6 1/3) instead of tripling it; only the 2 was multiplied.

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies the denominator too (12/32) or treats the problem additively; cannot see 5 × 1/4 as five quarters.
responseLevels.full: Computes n × a/b = (n×a)/b keeping the denominator fixed, multiplies every part of a mixed number, converts to a mixed-number answer, and justifies via repeated addition; transfers to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Gets fraction × whole by the rule (12/8) but falters on mixed numbers (incomplete distribution) or can't connect the rule to repeated addition of unit fractions.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing how you get each: 4 × 3/8, and 2 1/3 × 3. Write each answer as a mixed number where it helps.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who sees a/b as a multiple of the unit fraction multiplies only the count: 4 × 3/8 = twelve eighths, denominator fixed. Multiplying the denominator too (12/32) reveals the whole number is being wrongly applied to the size of the part. The mixed-number case exposes incomplete distribution — multiplying the whole but not the fraction part (6 1/3). Watching the working, not just the answer, shows whether the unit is held fixed and every part is scaled.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Area with Fractions
topic.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit-fraction squares; show that the area equals the product of the side lengths
evidence: Tile a 2/3 × 3/4 rectangle with 1/12 squares and count to find area = 6/12 = 1/2
Explain why the number of unit-fraction tiles equals the product of the two fractions
Calculate the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 using fraction multiplication
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a piece of fabric is 2/3 m long and 3/4 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area — and explain how tiling it with tiny fraction-squares shows the same answer as multiplying?

pedagogy.summary: Area with fractional side lengths is where the area model of fraction multiplication becomes a proof: a rectangle 2/3 unit by 3/4 unit, tiled with small squares, contains squares each worth 1/12 of a unit square (because the unit is cut into 3 columns and 4 rows → 12 tiles), and the shaded 2×3 = 6 of them give 6/12 = 1/2. The representational demand is to READ such a tiled diagram — say what one tile is worth and what multiplication the whole shows — and to PRODUCE one for a new product. The load-bearing insight is that the unit square is REDEFINED by the two partitions: denominators multiply because the tile count per unit is b×d, and numerators multiply because a×c tiles are shaded. This grounds (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd in an area a child can count.
bestPractices: Start from a whole unit square and partition it in TWO directions (vertical thirds, horizontal quarters) so the child sees 12 tiles appear and names each as 1/12 — the redefinition of the unit is the whole lesson
Connect the tile count to the symbols explicitly: 3×4 = 12 in the denominator is the tiles-per-unit; 2×3 = 6 in the numerator is the shaded tiles
Have children both interpret a given tiling AND draw their own for a fresh product, so reading and producing the representation are both secured
Use the area model to make simplification visible — 6/12 of the unit square is literally half of it, seen by eye
Extend to a mixed-number side (1 1/2 × 2/3) by tiling more than one unit square, so the model scales beyond proper fractions
Keep the unit square explicit and labelled throughout — the commonest failure is losing track of what '1' is
keyRepresentations: Two-way partitioned unit square (area model) with a×c tiles shaded out of b×d
Single unit-fraction tile labelled 1/(b×d) as the counting unit
Grid extended across several unit squares for mixed-number sides
Side-by-side diagram and equation (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd with the tiles that justify each factor
commonMisconceptions: Reads the tile as 1/(b+d) — e.g. 1/7 for a 3-by-4 partition — adding the partitions instead of multiplying (area treated additively)
Confuses area with perimeter — measures the boundary of the shaded rectangle rather than counting interior tiles
Partitions in only one direction, so the two-dimensional tile is never formed and denominators are not multiplied
Loses the unit square: counts shaded tiles as a whole number (6) rather than 6 of 12 of ONE unit
Believes area must be larger than the sides, so distrusts an area (1/2) smaller than either side length

learn.summary: Teaches area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths as a visual demonstration of fraction multiplication: a unit square cut in two directions (e.g. thirds one way, quarters the other) forms b×d tiles each worth 1/(b×d), and shading the a×c corner block gives ac/bd of the unit. The core insight is that the unit square is REDEFINED by the two partitions — denominators multiply because there are b×d tiles per unit, numerators multiply because a×c tiles are shaded. Learners must both READ a given tiled diagram (naming one tile's value and the multiplication it shows) and PRODUCE one for a fresh product. Worked example: 2/3 × 3/4 gives 3×4=12 tiles, 2×3=6 shaded = 6/12 = 1/2 — an area smaller than either side because both sides are less than 1.

activities.title: Build the area and watch the tiles appear
feedback: If a learner names the tile 1/7 (3 columns + 4 rows), pause and count the tiles in one unit square out loud together: 3 across, 4 down — the grid makes 12 tiles, not 7. The number of columns and the number of rows multiply (3 × 4 = 12); they do not add.
If a learner reports the edge of the shaded rectangle instead of the interior, distinguish 'how far around' from 'how much surface': point to and count the filling tiles, not the boundary.

If a learner is unsettled that 1/2 is smaller than both 2/3 and 3/4, show that taking a fraction (less than 1) OF another fraction gives a part of a part, so here it is smaller than either factor — the whole unit square is the reference, and the shaded block spans 2/3 of the width and 3/4 of the height, so it covers only half the whole square. (This 'smaller than both' result holds because both side lengths are less than 1; a mixed-number side such as 1 1/2 can give a larger product.)
Confirm success when the learner links 3×4 to the tile count/denominator and 2×3 to the shaded count/numerator, keeping the unit square as the named whole throughout.
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit square in two directions and counting the resulting tiles makes the redefinition of the unit visible and countable, grounding the symbolic rule in an area the learner can see and count. A live two-way tiler (vertical slider for thirds, horizontal slider for quarters, auto-labelled 1/12 tile, a shaded region reporting 6/12 = 1/2, and a 'show the whole unit' toggle that greys the other tiles) makes the recompute itself the proposed proof; such interactivity is one possible approach, not the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: The area model — partitioning a unit square in two directions so the unit is redefined into b×d tiles and a×c are shaded — is the recommended representation for developing understanding of fraction multiplication ((a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd)

Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths
learnerActions: Start from one whole unit square. Partition it in two directions — cut it into 3 columns one way and 4 rows the other way — to model 2/3 × 3/4.
Count the small tiles that appear in the whole unit square (3 across × 4 down = 12) and name the value of ONE tile: 1/12 of the unit square.
Shade the 2-by-3 corner block (2 of the 3 columns, 3 of the 4 rows) and count the shaded tiles: 2×3 = 6, so 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2.
Compare the shaded rectangle against the whole unit square and confirm it is exactly half of it — an area smaller than either side length (because each side is less than 1).
Say aloud which number in the picture gives the denominator (3×4 = 12 tiles per unit) and which gives the numerator (2×3 = 6 shaded tiles).
activities.intendedInsight: Cutting the unit square in two directions redefines the unit into b×d equal tiles (so denominators multiply) and the shaded a×c block gives the numerator — this is why (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, and why the product can be smaller than both sides when both sides are less than 1.

activities.title: Read a tiled diagram and justify each number
feedback: If a learner reads the whole as an addition or reads the boundary, re-ask what multiplication the SHADED interior shows and have them count filling tiles.

A lift-the-flap or tap interaction ('tap a tile → 1/12'; 'tap the shaded block → 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2'; 'tap the axes → 3 columns × 4 rows = 12') can confirm each justification; the 'why 1/12 and not 1/7?' flap targets the additive error directly.

This reading task secures recognition; recognising a correct diagram does not itself show the learner can build one, so follow it immediately with a drawing task where the learner constructs the representation.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given tiling isolates the READ half of the representational goal and lets tappable layers tie each visible feature to its symbol. This is a scaffold: recognising a correct diagram does not show the learner can build one, so it should be paired with a production task.
sourceClaims: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths
learnerActions: Look at a fully tiled 2/3 × 3/4 diagram. Point to one tile and state its value, then state the multiplication the whole shaded rectangle shows.
Answer: why is one tile 1/12 and not 1/7? Trace the two-way cut that creates the grid to justify your answer.
Point to the part of the picture that gives the 12 (3 columns × 4 rows) and the part that gives the 6 (the 2×3 shaded block).
Match the diagram to its equation (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, identifying the tiles that justify each factor.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a tiled area diagram means naming the counting unit (1/(b×d)) and recognising the shaded block as the product — the two-directional grid of 3 columns × 4 rows, not adding the columns and rows (3 + 4), is what makes each tile a twelfth.

activities.title: Produce your own diagram for a fresh product
feedback: If the drawing has parallel strips (cut in one direction only), prompt: 'the OTHER side also has to be cut — how many pieces that way?' Have the learner lay the second set of cuts and re-count the grid before reading the area.
If the learner writes 4/5 or 1/2 as the answer, point back to the tile value: there are 10 tiles per unit, so each is 1/10 and 4 of them is 4/10 = 2/5.
For the 1 1/2 × 2/3 extension, check that the grid spans a full unit plus a half-unit wide (and 2/3 tall), so tiles are counted across both unit squares; with tiles of 1/6 the area comes to 6/6 = 1.

A produce-mode on a two-way tiler (blank grid; learner builds the product; it checks tile worth and shaded count) or offline drawing both work; the point is that the learner constructs the two cuts, not selects from options.
activities.rationale: Producing a fresh diagram exposes whether the two-directional partition genuinely transferred or was only recognised; a learner who cuts in one direction only, or cannot choose the cuts, reveals that the unit-redefinition idea did not stick. Extending to a mixed-number side confirms the model scales beyond proper fractions. A fixed grid or recognition-only response cannot verify a freely produced diagram, so independent drawing is needed here.
sourceClaims: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths
learnerActions: On a blank unit square, DRAW a rectangle showing 1/2 × 4/5: choose the two cuts yourself — partition into 2 one way and 5 the other way.
Name what one tile is worth (1/10) and explain why: 2×5 = 10 tiles fill the unit.
Shade a 1-by-4 block (4 tiles) and read the area: 4/10 = 2/5.
Say which cuts produced the 10 and which shaded tiles produced the 4, pointing to each number in your own drawing.

Extend the model: tile across more than one unit square to find the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 (here the product is 1, larger than the 2/3 side — a useful check that the 'smaller than both' intuition only applies when both sides are less than 1).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing both partitions yourself — not just one — is what shows you own the idea that two cuts redefine the unit; the model scales to mixed numbers by tiling more than one unit square.

constraints: Keep the unit square explicit and labelled throughout — losing track of what '1' is is the commonest failure.

A static or tappable tiled diagram supports reading (naming the tile, identifying the multiplication) but cannot host the produce half; pair it with an actual drawing task where the learner chooses both cuts.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice on tile value, shading on a pre-partitioned grid) can check specific points — e.g. distinguishing 1/12 from 1/7 — but do not require the learner to construct or explain the representation, and cannot verify a freely produced diagram. Use them as checks, not as the main task.

Rectangular area here is a planar (flat) idea; a thin cutout or screen grid only approximates the represented ideal unit square (ideal figures have zero thickness, while real paper or card has slight thickness). Avoid 3D/volume renderings, which can misframe the unit-square idea being taught.
Start each build from the whole unit square and partition in TWO directions; a one-direction cut never forms the two-dimensional tile and does not multiply the denominators.

Interpreting and producing a tiled diagram is visual-spatial work; talk alone cannot display the two-way partition or capture the learner's drawing, though discussion can support the reasoning alongside the diagram.
The 'product is smaller than either side' intuition applies only when both side lengths are less than 1; do not state it unconditionally, since the mixed-number extension (1 1/2 × 2/3 = 1) breaks it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle drawn 2/3 of a unit wide and 3/4 of a unit tall, tiled with small equal squares. assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two moves — READ then PRODUCE — catch different failures. Reading the tile as 1/12 versus 1/7 separates the child who multiplies the partitions from the one who adds them; naming the multiplication as 2/3 × 3/4 (not, say, an addition or a perimeter) tests that the diagram is read as area. pedagogy.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction (and by a whole number), understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. The area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a square one way, then a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations are that you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition) and that the product of two proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part.
bestPractices: Read the product as 'of': 2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths, and model it as a fraction of a fraction.
Use the area/'redefine the unit' model (IES Fig 7): shade one fraction vertically, the other horizontally, the crosshatch is the product over the b×d grid.
Establish that you multiply numerators and denominators directly — explicitly contrast with addition, which needs a common denominator, to block the imported rule.
Use estimation/benchmarks so a product smaller than both factors is expected (1/2 of 1/2 is 1/4), refuting 'multiplication makes bigger'.
Simplify products and, where possible, simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers.
Fold in the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) as c/d with d = 1.

Believes the product must be bigger than the factors, so distrusts a smaller answer.
Computes the product but leaves it unsimplified (6/12 rather than 1/2).

learn.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction, understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. An area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a unit square one way, a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations: you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition), and the product of two nonzero proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part. The whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) folds in as c/d with d = 1: 2/3 of 4 means splitting 4 into 3 equal parts and taking 2 of them, which equals four copies of 2/3. For a whole number greater than 1, the product is larger than the fraction factor (for 1 it is equal, for 0 it is 0).

activities.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
feedback: If the overlap puzzles the learner, point to the two striped strips: the crosshatch is the region that is BOTH two-thirds and four-fifths-shaded — a smaller block inside both.
When a product like 6/12 appears, prompt: 'Can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' and check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 cover the same region.

A running 'is the answer bigger or smaller than each factor?' readout (where available) shows that for two PROPER fractions, taking part of a part gives a product smaller than either; note that the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) instead grows beyond the fraction factor 2/3, because it is repeated copies rather than a part of a part.
activities.rationale: A fraction of a fraction is exactly the two-way-shaded area model; partitioning both ways and highlighting the overlap makes 'product = crosshatched tiles' and 'smaller than each proper factor' concrete and manipulable. Letting the learner build and vary the shading, rather than view a finished picture, is where the understanding is constructed.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.

Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Shade 4/5 of a unit square with vertical stripes.
Shade 2/3 of the square with horizontal stripes, over the same region.
Watch the square rule itself into a 3×5 grid of fifteenths; count the crosshatched overlap (8 tiles) and read the product as 8/15.
Repeat for 3/4 × 2/3: see the overlap as 6 tiles out of 12, then use a simplify step to collapse 6/12 to 1/2 on the same picture.
Say each product in words using 'of': '2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths.'

Fold in a whole-number case: model 2/3 × 4 (as 2/3 × 4/1) using four unit squares, splitting each into thirds and shading 2/3 of each (equivalently, splitting the 4 wholes into 3 equal parts and taking 2), and read off 8 thirds = 8/3 = 2 2/3; optionally show the same on a number line, jumping 2/3 four times to land on 8/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying two proper fractions means taking a part of a part; the crosshatched overlap sits plainly INSIDE both striped regions, so the product is smaller than either proper factor, and the b×d grid gives the denominator automatically (no common denominator needed). The whole-number case is different: 2/3 × 4 is four copies of 2/3, so 8/3 is larger than 2/3.

activities.title: Contrast multiplication with the addition rule
feedback: If the learner keeps a denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3), model on the grid that 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block — 2/9 of the whole (2 tiles of 9), not 2/3.

If the learner hunts a common denominator first, ask which operation this is and whether equal-sized parts are needed to combine (that is addition); show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5 for 2/3 × 4/5.
activities.rationale: The leave-the-denominator and seek-a-common-denominator errors come from importing the addition schema. Explicitly contrasting the two operations on the same visual blocks the imported rule rather than just correcting the symbol manipulation.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 × 1/3 on the area grid: shade 1/3 one way, take 2/3 of it the other way, and count the overlap — 2 tiles out of 9, i.e. 2/9.
State explicitly: the answer is NOT 2/3; two-thirds OF one-third is smaller than one-third.

Compare side by side with an addition problem that needs re-partitioning (e.g. 2/3 + 4/5): notice addition needs same-sized parts (a common denominator) before you can combine, while multiplication splits the unit BOTH ways and the b×d grid supplies the denominator.
Explain in words why you do not need a common denominator to multiply.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication and addition of fractions run different procedures: addition needs a common denominator to combine like-sized parts; multiplication multiplies across because you are partitioning the unit in two directions.

activities.title: Compute and simplify (practice and self-check)
feedback: For a product that keeps an original denominator (e.g. 8/5 or 8/3 written for 2/3 × 4/5), point back to the grid: the tiles are fifteenths because the square was split 3×5, so the answer is 8/15.
For a correct but unsimplified answer (6/12), do not reteach the multiplication — it is right; only prompt for simplest form.
Use the benchmark 1/2 of 1/2 = 1/4 to confirm that a smaller-than-both answer is expected for two proper fractions, not an error.
activities.rationale: A scorable practice set can deliberately bait the leave-denominator and need-common-denominator errors and can isolate whether the simplifying step is secure. Recognition/fill-in items consolidate and diagnose; they check fluency rather than building the initial 'part of a part' concept, so they follow the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items of the form '2/3 × 4/5 = __/__ = __ (simplest form)'.
Answer a multiple-choice item for 2/3 × 1/3 where '2/3' (denominator left unchanged) is offered as a tempting wrong answer, and choose/justify the correct 2/9.
Finish a problem that yields 6/12 and reduce it to 1/2 as a required step.
Estimate before computing: predict whether each product is bigger or smaller than its factors.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency: multiply numerators and denominators directly, always put the result in simplest form, and expect the product of two proper fractions to be smaller than each factor.

constraints: Read every product as 'of' first (2/3 × 4/5 = two-thirds OF four-fifths) and model it before computing symbolically.
Explicitly contrast with addition: multiplication multiplies straight across and needs no common denominator; raise this whenever a learner tries to find one.
Always put products in simplest form, and where possible simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers (8/3 = 2 2/3).
The practice items check fluency and bait known errors; they do not by themselves build the 'part of a part' meaning, so pair them with the area-model construction rather than substitute for it.

A static finished picture (e.g. tapping to reveal 8/15 on a pre-shaded square) can serve as a reference anchor, but it does not let the learner build the shading or vary the factors, which is where the understanding forms — use it as a supplement, not the main activity.
The area model is planar; a flat grid is the natural representation here and a 3D rendering is not needed for this objective.

The claim 'product is smaller than either factor' is scoped to two nonzero proper fractions; when a proper fraction multiplies a whole number greater than 1, the product (e.g. 2/3 × 4 = 8/3) is smaller than the whole number but larger than the proper fraction factor.

pedagogy.summary: These real-world problems multiply fractions AND mixed numbers in context — scaling a recipe (2 1/3 cups × 1 1/2 batches), with estimation used to judge reasonableness. The signature difficulty is mixed-number multiplication: pupils who multiply the whole parts and the fraction parts separately and add (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6) omit the cross terms and get a badly wrong answer. The fix is to convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or to use an area model that shows ALL four partial products. Reasonableness via scaling (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 ≈ 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) is the check that catches the incomplete-distribution error.
bestPractices: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (2 1/3 = 7/3), avoiding incomplete distribution
Or use an area model for mixed × mixed that lays out ALL four partial products so none is dropped
Estimate by scaling before computing (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) and check the exact answer against it
Use the scaling meaning — more than one batch means MORE than 2 1/3 cups — to sense-check direction
Draw a fraction/area model of the context so the computation is grounded, not rote

Improper-fraction rewrite of both mixed numbers
Recipe/scaling bar showing the ingredient stretched by the batch factor
Estimation with rounded decimals or whole numbers

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 10–11) solve real-world problems multiplying fractions and mixed numbers, e.g. scaling a recipe of 2 1/3 cups by 1 1/2 batches. The signature error is incomplete distribution: multiplying whole×whole and fraction×fraction separately and adding (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6), which drops the two cross-term contributions. Fixes are converting both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or using an area model that shows ALL four partial products; a scaling estimate (≈2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) catches the error.

activities.title: Recipe scaler with a four-region area model
feedback: If the learner answers 2 1/6, point to the rectangle: the 2×1/2 and 1/3×1 strips — the biggest contributions after the main block — were left out. Ask them to add those regions in.
If a common-denominator step appears, note that this is a multiplication: both denominators multiply (3×2=6) and no common denominator is needed; contrast with how addition of fractions works.

If an out-of-range answer is accepted without doubt, ask: 'More than one batch means more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' — since 1 1/2 batches is more than one, the answer must exceed 2 1/3, so 2 1/6 is impossible.
Confirm success when the area total, the improper-fraction result, and the estimate all agree on about 3 1/2 cups.
activities.rationale: The incomplete-distribution error is literally a missing piece of an area, so an area model that displays and sums all four partial products is intended to make the omission visible and to tie the recipe context to the computation. An optional interactive version can light up or flash the two cross-term regions as uncounted when the shortcut is attempted, with a parallel improper-fraction panel and an estimate slider rounding to 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 — these are illustrative mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely

The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
learnerActions: Take a recipe needing 2 1/3 cups of flour and a goal of 1 1/2 batches, and first estimate by scaling (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) before doing any exact computation.
Draw or build a rectangle 2 1/3 wide and 1 1/2 tall to represent the product.
Tile the rectangle into its four regions: the 2×1 block, the 2×1/2 strip, the 1/3×1 strip, and the 1/3×1/2 corner; label each region's value (2, 1, 1/3, 1/6) and add them to get 3 1/2 cups.
Alongside, rewrite both mixed numbers as improper fractions and compute 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2, checking it matches the area total.
Check the exact answer (3 1/2 cups) against your earlier scaling estimate of about 3.5 cups.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed × mixed produces four partial products; the shortcut of only multiplying wholes and fractions omits the two large cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), so the answer 2 1/6 is far too small. Converting to improper fractions or counting all four regions gives the complete product, and a scaling estimate confirms direction and magnitude.

activities.title: Spot the forgotten pieces (static area diagram)
feedback: If the learner picks the small 1/3×1/2 corner as the 'forgotten' piece, point out the two long strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1) are the usually-dropped and far larger contributions.
Confirm when they name both cross-term strips and show the running total reaching 3 1/2.
activities.rationale: A static annotated diagram supports reading complete distribution and naming the typically omitted terms. It is a scaffold for interpretation; it does not by itself let the learner build a new product or catch their own omission while working, so it should precede or accompany independent construction rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely
learnerActions: Study a labelled area diagram of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 split into four regions.
Reveal each region's partial product in turn and keep a running total to 3 1/2 cups.
Answer: 'Which two pieces do people most often forget?' and explain why leaving them out gives 2 1/6.
activities.intendedInsight: Complete distribution means all four regions are counted; the commonly forgotten pieces are the two cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), which together are large enough that omitting them wrecks the answer.

activities.title: Chef scaling challenge (reasonableness in role)
feedback: If the learner assumes any multiplication increases the amount, use the 1/2-batch case: half a batch needs less than 2 1/3 cups, so the product is smaller.
Prompt them to state the direction before arithmetic so an out-of-range answer stands out.
activities.rationale: A spoken/role scenario is well suited to rehearsing the direction-of-scaling and reasonableness judgement and to confronting the 'multiplication makes bigger' misconception, including a less-than-one factor. The precise four-region computation still benefits from a visual surface, so pair this with the area or improper-fraction work rather than relying on discussion alone.
sourceClaims: The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
learnerActions: Work with a chef scenario that scales recipes up and down.
Before computing, answer 'more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' for a given batch factor and justify it.
Also tackle a shrinking case, e.g. making 1/2 a batch, and predict whether the flour needed is more or less than 2 1/3 cups.
Then compute the exact amount and check it against your prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling by more than one gives more than the original amount; scaling by a factor less than one gives less — so multiplication does not always make a number bigger. The reasonableness prediction is a check that catches implausible products.

activities.title: Targeted practice: convert, distribute, estimate
feedback: If 2 1/6 is chosen, revisit the two omitted cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1) and add them back in.
If 3 is chosen, point out it ignores or rounds away part of the fractional contributions; the full four-region total is 3 1/2, not 3.
If the conversion is wrong, remind them 2 1/3 = (2×3+1)/3 = 7/3.
Confirm when the learner selects 3 1/2, justifies it, and their estimate (≈3.5) supports it.
activities.rationale: Short-answer and matching items can probe whether conversion and complete distribution happened and whether an estimate was used, using the error patterns as sharp distractors. Such recognition-and-fill items assess and rehearse components but do not by themselves elicit the independent building of the area reasoning, so use them alongside the construction activities.
learnerActions: After first estimating the product by rounding (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5), choose the correct value of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 from 2 1/6, 3, and 3 1/2, and explain why the others are wrong.
Fill in the improper-fraction conversions: 2 1/3 = 7/3 and 1 1/2 = 3/2.
Match each of the four area regions to its partial product.
Estimate the product by rounding before carrying out the exact calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: The distractor 2 1/6 is exactly the incomplete-distribution result; 3 is a plausible wrong answer whose likely origin (rounding 2 1/3 down to 2, or dropping part of the fractional contribution) is not pinned down by the source, so it is used only as an explicitly-wrong option. Recognising why each is wrong reinforces complete distribution and the reasonableness check.

constraints: Target age 10–11; procedural real-world fraction and mixed-number multiplication.
Convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying, OR lay out all four partial products in an area model; do not multiply whole×whole and fraction×fraction and add.
This is multiplication: both denominators multiply and no common denominator is required — do not import addition/subtraction habits.

Require a scaling estimate before computing and check the exact answer against it; include at least one less-than-one (shrinking) factor so learners meet a case where the product is smaller than the original.

The static diagram and the recognition/matching items are scaffolds or checks: they support interpretation but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a new product or catch their own live omission.
The area model is a 2D representation of the product (cups × batches), not a physical area: cups of flour are actually a volume measure, but a 3D volume model is unnecessary and could mislead here.
Interactive touches (flashing uncounted regions, estimate slider, tappable regions) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory.
The '3' option is an explicitly-wrong distractor only; do not present it or 2 1/6 as a valid answer, and do not assert a certified origin for the '3' error beyond plausible rounding/omission.

The incomplete-distribution result 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6 is the stated misconception and is used only as an explicitly-wrong distractor, never as a valid answer.

The distractor '3' from the original quiz is retained as a plausible wrong option; its likely origin (rounding or dropping a term) is not specified in the source, so its exact diagnostic meaning is uncertain and is not asserted as fact.

probeDeeper: Estimate first — roughly how many cups? Does your exact answer match?
If you made only 1/2 a batch instead of 1 1/2, would you need more or less than 2 1/3 cups — why?
Draw the recipe as a rectangle — how many pieces are there, and did you count all of them?
Turn both mixed numbers into improper fractions — does multiplying them give the same answer as your method?

errorPatterns.pattern: Incomplete distribution: multiplies the whole parts and the fraction parts only — 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → (2×1) + (1/3×1/2) = 2 1/6 — omitting the two cross terms
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay out the area with all four regions (or convert both to improper fractions) so the two large cross-term strips are counted; check against the scaling estimate
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 2 1/6 (or similar too-small value); working shows only two products, no conversion to improper fractions

errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert to improper fractions first (7/3 × 3/2) and recall that multiplication multiplies both denominators and needs no common denominator; contrast with addition
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A common-denominator step appears in a multiplication, or the mixed numbers are multiplied part-wise with a kept denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Skips the reasonableness check — no estimate, so an implausible product (2 1/6, or a value below one batch) is accepted
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the scaling estimate — 'more than one batch, so more than 2 1/3 cups' — and require it before computing; the check, not the arithmetic, is what's missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No estimate offered; an out-of-range answer reported without doubt

responseLevels.full: Estimates by scaling, computes 3 1/2 via improper fractions or a complete area model, checks the exact answer against the estimate, and transfers to a new real-world product including a shrinking-factor (less-than-one) case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve this, showing your working and giving a rough estimate first: a recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour, and you want to make 1 1/2 batches — how much flour do you need?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Mixed × mixed is the exact place the incomplete-distribution error bites: a child who converts to improper fractions (or lays out all four partial products) gets 3 1/2; a child who multiplies whole×whole and fraction×fraction and adds gets 2 1/6 — and the estimate (≈3.5) instantly flags 2 1/6 as impossible. Requiring an estimate first plus the full working reveals both whether the distribution was complete and whether the answer was sense-checked, neither visible from a bare number.
