topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Multiplying fractions (age 11+)
topic.description: Interpret fractions and percentages as operators — find a fraction or percentage of an amount by multiplying, understanding that 'of' means multiply (e.g., 3/4 of 200 = 3/4 × 200 = 150)
evidence: Calculate a fraction of a given amount by multiplying
Calculate a percentage of a given amount by converting to a decimal and multiplying
Use the operator interpretation to solve multi-step problems involving discounts, taxes, and portions
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a £120 jacket is reduced by 35%, can {{name}} work out the sale price — by first calculating 35% of £120 and then subtracting?

pedagogy.summary: 'Finding a fraction or percentage OF an amount' is the operator interpretation of multiplication: 'of' means multiply. The prior 'a/b of q' work becomes fully general here — 3/4 of 200 = 3/4 × 200 = 150; 20% of 60 = 0.2 × 60 = 12. The pedagogical crux is that children fluent in unit-fraction-of (÷ by denominator) must generalise to non-unit fractions and to percentages, and must accept that multiplying can make a quantity SMALLER. Teach it as one operator acting on a quantity — bar/hundred-grid partition first, then the ×-as-operator equation — and anchor it in real contexts (discounts, tax, portions) where the operator chains.
bestPractices: Build from the known unit-fraction case: to find 3/4 of 200, first find 1/4 (÷4 = 50) then take 3 of them (×3 = 150); make the two-step structure explicit before compressing to 3/4 × 200
Represent the amount as a whole bar or a hundred-grid and physically partition it, so 'of' is seen as partition-then-take, matching the (a/b)×q meaning
Convert percentages to fractions/decimals deliberately (20% = 20/100 = 0.2) so 'percentage of' reuses the identical operator, not a separate rule
Use realistic multi-step contexts — 20%-off a £45 jacket, VAT, tips, recipe portions — so the operator is chained and the answer's reasonableness can be judged
Contrast a scaling-up operator (150% of, 5/4 of) with a scaling-down one so children see 'of' is not tied to 'gets smaller'
keyRepresentations: Bar model of the whole amount partitioned into b equal parts, a of them shaded
Hundred-grid / percentage bar for percentage-of
Double number line pairing the amount with 0-100% for percentage-of
The operator equation a/b × q, written beside the partition it summarises
commonMisconceptions: Finds the unit fraction and stops (200÷4 = 50 offered as '3/4 of 200'), forgetting to take a copies
Converts the percentage wrongly — 25% treated as ÷25 or ×25, or 20% as 0.02 / 2.0
Believes 'of'/multiplication must enlarge, so distrusts a correct smaller answer
Adds/subtracts the percentage directly to the amount instead of operating (20% of 60 read as 60+20 or 60-20)

learn.summary: Teach 'a fraction/percentage OF an amount' as one multiplicative operator: 'of' means multiply. Build from the known unit-fraction case (3/4 of 200 = find 1/4 by ÷4 = 50, then take 3 = 150), make percentage-of reuse the identical operator via conversion (20% = 20/100 = 0.2, so 20% of 60 = 0.2×60 = 12), and anchor it in real discount/tax/portion contexts. The conceptual crux is accepting that multiplying can make a quantity smaller when the operator is below 1, while an operator above 1 grows it. Visual partition (bar, hundred-grid, double number line) should precede and sit beside the ×-as-operator equation.

activities.title: Operator machine: set an amount, set an operator, watch it partition
feedback: If a learner stops at the unit fraction (gives 50 for 3/4 of 200), re-shade ONE quarter (50) then ask 'how many quarters is three-quarters?' and shade the other two before recompressing to 3/4 ×.
If a learner expects the answer to always be bigger, direct them to flip the operator past 1 and back under 1 and compare each result with the starting amount.
If '20% off £45' is answered as 45 − 20 = £25, insist the operator acts ON the price: find 20% OF 45 first (= £9), shade it, then take it away.
activities.rationale: Setting the amount, choosing the operator and seeing the live partition makes the partition-then-take meaning concrete and lets the learner test the 'does of always shrink?' question directly; chaining a real discount shows the operator applied in context. The shrink/grow toggle and live recolouring are offered as one interaction example to make the mechanism visible, not as the only valid medium.

Fractions and ratios function as operators/multipliers on quantities (a/b of q = a/b × q); percentage of a quantity is the same operator via decimal conversion

By age 11 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures and money) and find fractions of amounts using multiplication; 'of' as an operator is a Year 6 / KS3 expectation
learnerActions: Enter an amount shown as a whole bar or hundred-grid (e.g. 200).

Work one example at a time, each with its own entered amount: with 200 in the bar apply the fraction 3/4; then re-enter 60 and apply the percentage 20% — watch the same machine partition into equal parts and shade the taken portion each time.
Read the equation printed beside each partition: 3/4 × 200 = 150; and separately 20% = 20/100 = 0.2, so 0.2 × 60 = 12.
Move the operator above 1 (e.g. 150% of 200 = 300, or 5/4 of 200 = 250) and below 1, and describe in words whether the result grew or shrank from the starting amount and why.

Second stage — a shop: start from a £45 price, apply '20% off' so 20% of £45 = £9 is shaded (a double number line pairing £0–£45 with 0–100% can show where 20% sits), then subtract to reach the £36 paid; state the two separate moves — find 20% OF the price, THEN take it away.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Of' is one action — partition the whole into equal parts, then take a copies — whether it wears a fraction hat or a percent hat. Whether the result is bigger or smaller than you started is decided by the operator's size, not by multiplication 'always enlarging'.

activities.title: Worked bar in stages: make the two-step structure inspectable
feedback: If only the ÷denominator step appears, ask what the numerator tells you to do with the unit parts you found.
If the 'why smaller' prompt stalls, point to how many of the four parts were taken versus how many make the whole.
activities.rationale: A staged, revealable worked example exposes the hidden two-step structure that fluent learners often compress, and a parallel percentage bar shows the operator reused. A fixed worked example of this kind supports inspection of structure; it does not let the learner vary the operator themselves, so pair it with exploratory or production work.
sourceClaims: Finding a fraction of a fraction / of a quantity is fraction multiplication, and multiplying can produce a result smaller than the starting amount — a documented source of student surprise the operator interpretation must confront
Fractions and ratios function as operators/multipliers on quantities (a/b of q = a/b × q); percentage of a quantity is the same operator via decimal conversion
learnerActions: On a whole bar for 3/4 of 200, split it into four equal parts and name one part (1/4 = 50).
Take (shade) three of those parts and record the second move explicitly (×3 → 150).

Repeat the same staged partition on a hundred-grid for 20% of 60, reading '20 of the hundred parts' and reaching 12; a double number line pairing 60 with 0–100% can sit alongside to show 20% as a position.
Answer the prompt 'why is the answer smaller than 200?' in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a non-unit fraction of an amount is two linked steps — divide to find the unit part, then multiply to take a copies — and percentage-of is the same partition read out of a hundred.

activities.title: In-role market trader: reasoning about more-or-less
feedback: If the learner detaches the percentage from the price, ask 'twenty percent OF what?' before any subtraction.
If they claim the £-off stays the same when the price doubles, have them compute 20% of £90 (= £18) and compare with 20% of £45 (= £9).
activities.rationale: Spoken reasoning and responsive challenge can elicit and probe the shrink/scale intuition and the reasonableness judgement; keep numbers small enough for mental work. Discussion complements rather than replaces the visual partitioning and written computation, which benefit from a visual surface. No source establishes dialogue as superior to another medium here, so this is a qualified proposal.
learnerActions: Take on a market-trader/shopkeeper exchange where you compute successive small-number discounts and portions mentally.
Before each calculation, answer the trader's probe: 'is that more or less than you started with?'
Explain to the trader what the money taken off actually is — e.g. '£9 is 20% OF the £45 price'.
Reason about a what-if: if the price doubled from £45 to £90, would the £-off double? Justify (20% of £90 = £18, double the £9).
activities.intendedInsight: The operator is applied to a specific quantity, so the amount taken off scales with that quantity; judging reasonableness ('more or less than I started') is part of operating correctly.

activities.title: Mixed operator check with targeted distractors
feedback: Choosing 50 flags the missing ×numerator step — return to taking three of the quarters.
Landing on 3, 120 or 1.2 flags a conversion fault — rebuild 20% = 20/100 = 0.2 on a hundred-grid.
Landing on £25 flags subtracting the raw percentage — find 20% OF 45 (= £9) first, then subtract.
activities.rationale: A scored check with distractors built from the documented error patterns (unit-fraction-stop, percentage mis-conversion, operate-vs-subtract confusion) surfaces which specific operator move is broken. Such a check verifies fluency and diagnoses faults; selecting a correct option does not itself elicit independent construction, so it should follow the construction and visual activities rather than replace them.
learnerActions: Set 1/4 of 200, then choose 3/4 of 200 from options that include the unit-fraction-stop value 50.
Complete the conversion 20% = 0.__ then compute × 60, with options reflecting common mis-conversions (3, 120, 1.2) alongside the correct 12.
Solve a discount word step for the £45 jacket with distractors £25 (from 45−20) and other near-value options alongside the correct £36, showing the 20%-of-45 = £9 step.
Read the feedback given after each item, which names which operator move was right or wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Operating correctly means completing BOTH the divide and the take-a-copies step, converting the percentage cleanly, and operating-then-subtracting in a discount — not pattern-matching to a single rule.

constraints: Build from the known unit-fraction case before compressing: make the two-step structure (÷denominator to find the unit part, then ×numerator to take a copies) explicit for non-unit fractions.
Convert percentages deliberately (20% = 20/100 = 0.2) so percentage-of reuses the identical operator rather than becoming a separate rule.
Deliberately contrast an operator below 1 (shrinks) with one above 1 (grows, e.g. 150% of, 5/4 of) so learners do not glue 'multiply' to 'gets bigger'.

Keep each operator example's amount explicit so the printed equation matches the amount actually set (e.g. 3/4 of 200, 20% of 60, 20% of £45) — do not silently change the amount between a stated setup and its result.
Use realistic multi-step contexts (discount, VAT, tips, recipe portions) and require judging the answer's reasonableness.

The staged worked bar is a scaffold: it makes structure inspectable but the learner cannot vary the operator, so it must not be the only format — pair it with activity where the learner sets the operator and with production tasks.
The scored check assesses and diagnoses fluency; it does not by itself build the operator meaning and should follow, not replace, the constructive work.
Recognition/multiple-choice responses do not elicit independent construction; include tasks where the learner computes and shows method, not only selects an answer.
Discount tasks require two distinct moves — find the percentage OF the amount, then subtract — and both should be stated separately.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the two-step structure on a bar: shade ONE quarter (50), then ask 'how many quarters is three-quarters?' and shade the other two; make 'a copies of the unit part' explicit before recompressing to 3/4 ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 50 for 3/4 of 200 (or divides by the numerator), method shows the ÷denominator step but not the ×numerator step

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-converts the percentage: treats 20% as ×20, ÷20, 2.0 or 0.02 rather than 0.2 — 'per cent means out of a hundred' not carried into the operator ('20% of 60 is 60 ÷ 20 = 3' or '× 20 = 1200')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 20% = 20/100 = 0.2 on a hundred-grid and read '20 of the hundred parts of 60'; connect back to percentage-as-fraction before re-attempting

responseLevels.gap: Cannot connect 'of' to multiplication: gives 50, or subtracts the percentage as a number, or cannot start the discount; treats each item as an unrelated rule.
responseLevels.full: Operates fluently across fraction-of, percentage-of and the multi-step discount, converting the percentage cleanly and judging the answer's reasonableness; explains that 'of' = × and that an operator below 1 shrinks and above 1 grows, transferring the same machine to an unfamiliar context.
responseLevels.partial: Operates correctly on straightforward cases (3/4 of 200 = 150, 20% of 60 = 12) but the method is a memorised procedure — cannot say why the answer may be smaller, or stumbles on the discount because operate-then-subtract is not seen as the SAME operator applied to a context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out and show your method for each: first, 3/4 of 200; then 20% of 60. Now a real one — a jacket costs £45 and it has 20% off in a sale. What do you pay?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the METHOD separates the child who genuinely operates from the one who pattern-matches: the 3/4 case exposes whether they take all three quarters or stop at the unit fraction; the 20% case exposes their percentage-to-operator conversion; and the discount forces them to operate THEN subtract, so a child who just does 45−20 or 45−9-without-the-9-being-20%-of-45 reveals a broken operator. topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Dividing by 10 and 100
topic.description: Find the effect of dividing a one- or two-digit number by 10 and 100, identifying the value of the digits as ones, tenths, and hundredths
evidence: Calculate 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and identify 3 as ones and 7 as tenths
Calculate 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 and identify 4 as hundredths
Explain that dividing by 10 shifts each digit one place to the right
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts with the number 48 and divides it by 10, can they tell you the answer — and explain what happened to each digit's place value?

pedagogy.summary: Dividing by 10 (or 100) makes every digit ten (or a hundred) times smaller, so each digit slides one place (or two places) to the RIGHT on a place-value chart while the digits themselves and their order stay the same. 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 from ones to tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (the 4 moves to hundredths and a zero must hold the empty tenths place). It is emphatically NOT 'move the decimal point' or 'add/remove a zero' — those rules mislead as soon as a placeholder is needed.
bestPractices: Use a place-value chart and physically slide digit cards one column right per division by 10 — the digits move, the point stays put
Forbid the 'just add/cross off a zero' shortcut; it only works for multiples of ten and breaks on 37 ÷ 10
Make the placeholder zero explicit: for 4 ÷ 100 the tenths column is empty, so a 0 must hold it to give 0.04, not 0.4
Anchor in money and metric (£4 ÷ 100 = 4p = £0.04; 37 cm ÷ 10) so the shrinking is meaningful
Read every result back by place value ('3 ones and 7 tenths') rather than as a digit string
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with sliding/draggable digit cards
Gattegno (tenths/hundredths) chart
Base-ten blocks with exchange (a rod is a tenth of a flat)
Number line and money/metric contexts
commonMisconceptions: Applies 'move the decimal point' by rote and gets the magnitude wrong (37 ÷ 10 → 0.37 or 370)
Omits the placeholder zero: 4 ÷ 100 → 0.4
Over-generalises 'divide by 10 = take a zero off', which fails on numbers without a trailing zero

learn.summary: Dividing by 10 or 100 makes every digit ten or a hundred times smaller, so each digit slides one or two places to the RIGHT on a place-value chart while the digits and their order stay the same. 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 from ones to tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (the 4 moves to hundredths and a 0 must hold the empty tenths place). The reliable idea is that digits shift and shrink. 'Add/remove a zero' fails for numbers like 37, which have no trailing zero, and 'move the decimal point' gives the same answer but hides why the values change and can lead to errors when a placeholder is needed.

activities.title: Slide the digits right on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 0.37 or 370 for 37 ÷ 10, return to the chart and slide each digit exactly one column right; show the point stays put and the digits move, and ask 'ten times smaller than 37 — is that near 3 or near 300?'

If a learner writes 0.4 for 4 ÷ 100, show the 4 landing in hundredths with the tenths column empty; ask what must hold the empty tenths place, and establish that without the 0 the value would be ten times too big.
When a learner reads results by digit string, prompt them to name each digit's place value instead ('what is the 7 worth now?').
activities.rationale: The concept is literally a movement of digits across columns, so enacting the slide and naming each landing place targets magnitude and placeholder reasoning directly, rather than a memorised symbol rule.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal place value stem from over-generalising whole-number rules (e.g. 'add/remove a zero', 'move the point') rather than reasoning about the size of each digit's place; secure understanding requires reasoning about place value, not memorised digit-manipulation rules.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns labelled hundreds, tens, ones, then a decimal point, then tenths and hundredths.
Place digit cards for 37 (3 in tens, 7 in ones) and predict what dividing by 10 will do.
Divide by 10 by sliding each digit card one column to the RIGHT: the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 moves from ones to tenths, giving 3.7. Notice the decimal point itself does not move.
Read the result back by place value: '3 ones and 7 tenths'.
Now place a single digit card for 4 in the ones column and divide by 100 by sliding it two columns right, so the 4 lands in hundredths.
Notice the tenths column is now empty and write a 0 to hold that place, giving 0.04. Say why, without the 0, you would wrongly read 0.4.

Optionally model the same shrink with another representation — base-ten blocks with exchange (letting a flat be one whole so a rod is a tenth of a flat and a small cube a hundredth), a Gattegno tenths/hundredths chart, or a number line — to see the quantity becoming ten or a hundred times smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 (or 100) shifts every digit one (or two) places right and makes it ten (or a hundred) times smaller; a placeholder zero is needed whenever a column between the point and a digit is left empty.

activities.title: Confront the 'take a zero off' rule
feedback: If a learner stalls trying to remove a zero from 37, point to the pair 40 ÷ 10 (works) versus 37 ÷ 10 (fails) and rebuild using the digit slide.
If a learner keeps 37 unchanged, ask 'is your answer ten times smaller than 37?' to expose the error.
activities.rationale: Directly comparing a case where the shortcut appears to work against one where it breaks helps dislodge the over-generalised whole-number rule, which is the documented source of error.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal place value stem from over-generalising whole-number rules (e.g. 'add/remove a zero', 'move the point') rather than reasoning about the size of each digit's place; secure understanding requires reasoning about place value, not memorised digit-manipulation rules.
learnerActions: Work out 40 ÷ 10 and notice that 'take a zero off' happens to give 4.
Now try the same rule on 37 ÷ 10 and show it fails — there is no trailing zero to remove, and leaving 37 unchanged (or writing 370) is wrong.
Redo 37 ÷ 10 on the place-value chart by sliding digits right to get 3.7, and state in your own words why the shortcut only worked for 40.

Test 'move the decimal point' similarly and check it against the chart result. Notice that, done correctly, it agrees with the chart, but it does not show that each digit has become ten times smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Remove a zero' only works when there is a trailing zero to remove, and 'move the point' gives the right result only when it is applied carefully but does not explain why it works. Sliding each digit one place right and reading place value always works and shows why.

activities.title: Anchor the shrink in money and measurement
feedback: If a learner gives £0.4 for £4 ÷ 100, relate it to coins: 4p is four hundredths of a pound, so a 0 must hold the tenths (ten-pence) place.
Have the learner read each answer by place value to confirm the magnitude is sensible.
activities.rationale: Familiar money and metric contexts make the shrinking meaningful and give a concrete check on magnitude and placeholder placement.
learnerActions: Work out £4 ÷ 100 and connect it to 4p, writing it as £0.04; check the 4 sits in the hundredths (pence-of-a-pound) place.
Work out 37 cm ÷ 10 and express the result as 3.7 cm, checking which column each digit lands in.
For each context, say which digit moved and what it is now worth.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 or 100 means a quantity becomes ten or a hundred times smaller, and the place-value result matches real money and metric amounts.

activities.title: Check placeholder and magnitude with targeted questions
feedback: If 0.4 is chosen for 4 ÷ 100, show on the chart that the 4 belongs in hundredths and the tenths place needs a 0.
If 0.004 is chosen, check how many columns the 4 moved: dividing by 100 moves it two places, not three.
Confirm understanding by asking the learner to name each digit's place value, not just the numeral.
activities.rationale: Well-chosen distractors (0.4 for the missing placeholder, 0.004 for over-shifting) surface the exact magnitude and placeholder errors; this checks whether a result is correct and should follow, not replace, the hands-on slide work.
learnerActions: Complete 37 ÷ 10 = ___ and state what each digit is worth.
Choose the correct value of 4 ÷ 100 from 0.4, 0.04, and 0.004, and justify the choice by naming where the 4 lands.
Match each digit in your answers to its place value (ones, tenths, hundredths).
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer must place every digit in the right column, using a placeholder zero where a column is emptied; the 0.4-versus-0.04 distinction is the sharpest test.

activities.title: Static chart as a reference label
feedback: If a learner can label landing places but cannot produce them, return to physically sliding the digits so the movement is performed, not just read.
activities.rationale: A still reference supports vocabulary and recall; because it does not enact the slide, it works best alongside an activity where the learner carries out the movement.
learnerActions: Beside the moving chart, keep a labelled still chart and point to where each digit of 37 starts and where it lands after ÷10.
Use it to look up and name the place value of any digit in a result (for example, the hundredths place in 0.04).
activities.intendedInsight: A fixed chart names where digits land and supports recall of place-value labels, as a companion to enacting the movement.

constraints: Teach digits-shift-right with the decimal point staying fixed; do not teach 'add/remove a zero' as a rule, since it fails for any number without a trailing zero (e.g. 37 ÷ 10), and do not teach 'move the decimal point' as the main rule, since it gives the same result but hides why each digit's value changes and can lead to errors when a placeholder zero is needed (e.g. 4 ÷ 100).
Always make the placeholder zero explicit: 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04, not 0.4; require learners to say why the tenths place needs a 0.
Have learners read results by place value ('3 ones and 7 tenths'), not as a bare digit string, so magnitude is checked.
A static chart labels landing places but does not perform the movement; use it as a reference beside activities where the learner actually slides the digits.
Recognition/selection questions check whether a result is correct but do not by themselves elicit the learner independently constructing the movement; pair them with hands-on chart work.

Alternative representations (base-ten blocks with exchange, Gattegno chart, number line) are optional supports, not requirements; when using base-ten blocks, fix which block is the whole so a rod reads as a tenth.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source supports that decimal place-value errors arise from over-generalising whole-number rules and that place-value reasoning is needed; it does not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity or medium here.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 are correct; £4 ÷ 100 = £0.04 = 4p and 37 cm ÷ 10 = 3.7 cm are correct. The 0.004 distractor corresponds to an over-shift of three places (effectively ÷1000) and is retained only as an incorrect option, never as a valid answer.
The legacy source rated depth/3D and dialogue formats as adding nothing; that is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been dropped rather than asserted as universal.
The legacy reteach-prerequisite links for the error patterns use internal topic identifiers and were not migrated into learner-facing guidance.

The original keyRepresentations listed a Gattegno chart, base-ten blocks with exchange (a rod is a tenth of a flat), and a number line; these had been dropped by the candidate and have been restored as optional alternative representations.

probeDeeper: When you divide by 10, does each digit get bigger or smaller — and by how much?
In your answer 3.7, what is the 7 worth now, and where was that digit before?
For 4 ÷ 100, why can't we just write 0.4? What has to go in the tenths place, and why?
Some people say 'to divide by 10, take off a zero'. Does that work for 37 ÷ 10? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (3 ones, 7 tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (4 hundredths, with 0 holding the tenths place). Explains that dividing by 10 shifts every digit one place to the right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the decimal point by rule without place-value meaning, landing the wrong magnitude: 37 ÷ 10 → 0.37 or 370
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go to the place-value chart and slide the digits one column right; show the point stays and the digits move. Rebuild what 'ten times smaller' means.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about 'moving the point' rather than 'each digit gets smaller'; answer is off by a factor of ten or a hundred

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the placeholder zero: 4 ÷ 100 → 0.4 because they 'put the 4 after the point'
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the chart, show the 4 landing in hundredths with the tenths column empty; a 0 must hold that place or the value is ten times too big.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.4 for 4 ÷ 100; cannot say what belongs in the tenths column

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'to divide by 10 just take a zero off' and is stuck or invents a zero when the number has none (37)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the rule directly: show 40 ÷ 10 where it seems to work and 37 ÷ 10 where it fails; replace it with digits-shift-right on the chart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tries to remove a zero from 37 and stalls, or writes 37 unchanged / 3.70

responseLevels.gap: Moves the point by rote or adds/removes zeros, producing the wrong magnitude, and cannot name the digits' place values.
responseLevels.full: Divides by 10 and 100 fluently with correct placeholder zeros, states each digit's new place value, and explains that dividing by 10 shifts every digit one place right; transfers to a fresh number.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 but fumbles 4 ÷ 100 (omits the placeholder or is unsure), or can name new place values only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a place-value chart and say: 'Work out 37 ÷ 10, then 4 ÷ 100. For each answer, tell me what each digit is worth.' Watch how they get the answer — do not tell them a method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands slides the digits right and keeps them, using a placeholder zero where a column is emptied (4 ÷ 100 = 0.04). A child running a rote 'move the point' or 'add/remove a zero' rule produces 0.37, 370, or 0.4. The 4 ÷ 100 case is the sharpest: it forces a placeholder zero that a rule-follower typically omits, and it asks for digit values, exposing whether place value is understood or just recited.

sources.claim: Errors in decimal place value stem from over-generalising whole-number rules (e.g. 'add/remove a zero', 'move the point') rather than reasoning about the size of each digit's place; secure understanding requires reasoning about place value, not memorised digit-manipulation rules.

topic.name: Dividing by Fractions
topic.description: Interpret and compute division of a whole number by a unit fraction (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain why the quotient is larger than the dividend
evidence: Compute 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 and explain: 'How many fifths fit in 4 wholes?'
Create a story context for 6 ÷ (1/4) and solve it
Verify 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 by showing 20 × (1/5) = 4
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you have 4 metres of ribbon and each bow needs 1/5 of a metre, can {{name}} work out how many bows you can make — and explain why the answer is bigger than 4?

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the MEASUREMENT (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' — each whole holds 5, so 4 hold 20. The whole pedagogical battle is that the answer is BIGGER than the number you started with, which collides head-on with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a number line or ribbon, reason with estimation ('5 ÷ 5/6 is a bit more than 5 because 5/6 is nearly 1'), and cement it with the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.
bestPractices: Lead with the 'how many fit' question on a length model — lay 1/5 ribbons or number-line jumps across 4 wholes and count them to 20 — so the quotient is something the child physically counts, not computes
Confront 'division makes smaller' head-on: predict the count first, then fit the pieces and see it exceed the dividend; discuss WHY (small divisor → many copies)
Use estimation to police reasonableness (IES: 5 ÷ 5/6 ≈ just over 5) so an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is caught as absurd
Always tie back to the inverse: 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20 because 20 × 1/5 = 4 — the multiplication just learned justifies the division
Have children invent a story context ('how many 1/4-cup scoops in 6 cups?') so the measurement structure is owned, not memorised
keyRepresentations: Number line partitioned into fifths with jumps counted across 0–4
Ribbon/tape model: unit-fraction lengths laid end-to-end inside the whole (IES Fig 8 style)
Array of unit-fraction pieces filling the dividend
The inverse equation 20 × 1/5 = 4 written beside the count
commonMisconceptions: Quotient must be smaller than the dividend, so 4 ÷ 1/5 'can't' be 20 (whole-number over-generalisation that division shrinks)
Divides by the denominator instead: 4 ÷ 1/5 read as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 (treats the unit fraction as its denominator)
Confuses with multiplication: computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 (imports the more-familiar operation)
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers rather than 1/5 as one quantity

learn.summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the measurement (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 4 wholes hold 20. The central challenge is that the quotient is BIGGER than the dividend, which collides with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a length model, using prediction then counting, estimation to police reasonableness, and the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.

activities.title: How many fit? Predict then count on a length bar
feedback: If a learner predicts 'fewer than 4 because dividing shrinks', treat it as the teachable moment: lay the tiles and count to 20 together, then name the principle — a small divisor means many copies fit.
If a learner reads 4 ÷ 1/5 as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, rebuild what 1/5 IS (one part of a whole split five ways) and re-ask 'how many of THOSE fit in 4?'
If a learner computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5, separate the two questions explicitly: '4 × 1/5 means four fifths; 4 ÷ 1/5 means how many fifths in four', and model both on the same bar.
activities.rationale: The measurement/quotitive meaning is made concrete by fitting unit-fraction pieces into the dividend and counting them, with a length/ribbon or number-line model. Prediction-first surfaces the 'division shrinks' misconception so it can be confronted directly.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness

The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
learnerActions: Take a 4-unit strip/bar and a stack of 1/5 tiles (ribbon lengths or number-line jumps work equally well).
BEFORE placing any tile, write down a prediction of how many 1/5 tiles will fit, and a one-sentence reason.
Lay the 1/5 tiles end-to-end across the bar, counting as you go: 5 fill the first whole, 10 the second, and so on until you reach 20.
Compare the count (20) with your prediction, and discuss why the answer is bigger than 4.
Repeat with a different piece size (e.g. 1/2 gives 8, 1/10 gives 40) and describe how the size of the piece drives the count.
activities.intendedInsight: When the piece is small, many copies fit, so dividing a positive whole number by a fraction between 0 and 1 produces a count larger than the dividend. The quotient is something you can physically count, not a trick.

activities.title: Estimate first to catch absurd answers
feedback: If a learner cannot say whether the answer grows or shrinks, return to the 'how many fit' question with a concrete piece.
Praise reasoning that ties the estimate to the piece size relative to 1 whole (e.g. 'the piece is nearly a whole, so a bit more than 5').
activities.rationale: IES recommends estimation to police the reasonableness of fraction computations, which directly guards against the counterintuitive-result errors.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
learnerActions: Before computing, estimate whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the dividend, and roughly how big.
Work an example like 5 ÷ 5/6: reason that because 5/6 is nearly 1 whole, the answer is a little more than 5.
Check a worked answer for reasonableness: decide whether 0.8 could possibly be the answer to 4 ÷ 1/5, and explain why not.
State a rule of thumb: dividing by a piece smaller than 1 gives more copies than the number of wholes.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation acts as a reasonableness check: an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is immediately caught as absurd because many small fifths must fit in 4 wholes.

activities.title: Prove it with the inverse multiplication
feedback: If a learner cannot form the inverse, prompt: 'If 20 fifths make up 4, what multiplication says that?'
If the inverse product does not rebuild the dividend, revisit the count rather than accepting the quotient.
activities.rationale: Using the multiplication–division relationship to explain and verify the quotient is a core standard-aligned goal and avoids rote rule use.
sourceClaims: Interpret and compute quotients of whole numbers by unit fractions (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division; explain why the quotient is larger
learnerActions: After counting 20 fifths in 4 wholes, write the matching multiplication: 20 × 1/5 = 4.
Explain in words how the multiplication just learned justifies the division answer.
Gather or redraw the 20 fifths into 4 wholes to show the multiplication rebuilding the original dividend.
Apply the same check to a fresh case, e.g. verify 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 by showing 24 × 1/4 = 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Division by a unit fraction and the related multiplication are inverse statements about the same quantity, so the multiplication check confirms the division.

activities.title: Invent and solve a measurement story
feedback: If a learner's story does not match a 'how many small pieces fit in a whole amount' structure, help reshape it before solving.
Draw out the prediction step: a learner who expects fewer scoops has surfaced the shrink misconception, which the count then resolves.
activities.rationale: Creating and solving a story context cements the quotitive 'how many fit' measurement meaning; a measuring/cooking persona can pose the prediction challenge, though the counting itself benefits from a visual or physical surface.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
learnerActions: Invent a real context for a whole ÷ unit-fraction, e.g. 'how many 1/4-cup scoops are in 6 cups?' or 'how many 1/3-cup scoops in this jug?'
Before counting, predict out loud whether there will be more or fewer scoops than the number of whole cups, and say why.
Solve the story by counting the pieces and state the answer with its meaning.
Match several division expressions (e.g. 6 ÷ 1/4, 4 ÷ 1/5) to the correct 'how many … in …' story.
activities.intendedInsight: Owning the measurement structure through a self-made context makes the 'how many fit' meaning transferable rather than memorised.

activities.title: Check your understanding (prediction, count, and reasoning)
feedback: If a learner picks an answer smaller than the dividend, return to fitting pieces and the piece-size-drives-count principle.
If a learner picks a denominator-division distractor (e.g. treating 6 ÷ 1/4 as 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5), rebuild what the unit fraction is.
If the number is right but the reason is missing or rote, treat it as partial and probe the 'why bigger than the dividend' explanation.
activities.rationale: Recognition and ordering items can test the counterintuitive 'bigger answer' and the divisor-vs-denominator error; requiring the reason guards against rote recall passing as understanding. Selecting answers checks the misconception but does not by itself elicit the independent construction and explanation developed in the earlier activities.
sourceClaims: The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
learnerActions: Answer 'how many 1/5 fit in 4?' using a number-line count or slider, giving 20.

Answer a multiple-choice item for 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24, ruling out derivable distractors such as 1.5 (from the denominator-division error 6 ÷ 4) and a value smaller than the dividend (from the 'division shrinks' misconception).
Order several whole ÷ unit-fraction quotients by size to expose the 'answer must be smaller' misconception.
For any answer, add a sentence saying WHY it is bigger than the dividend; a correct number without a correct reason is incomplete.
activities.intendedInsight: A genuine grasp of the measurement meaning produces both the right quotient AND a 'how many fit' justification; recalling a number alone is not sufficient.

constraints: Lead with the 'how many fit' measurement question on a length model; the quotient should be something the child physically counts, not a rule they apply.
Confront 'division makes smaller' directly: predict first, then fit pieces and see the count exceed the dividend, then discuss why (small divisor → many copies).
Always tie back to the inverse check (20 × 1/5 = 4); do not teach an invert-and-multiply rule without this meaning.

A static number-line image showing 4 wholes cut into fifths with 20 countable segments supports the meaning well, but does not let the learner vary the divisor to test the pattern; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the misconception but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and explanation; pair them with activities that require counting and justifying.

Optional interactive supports (e.g. dragging 1/5 tiles into a bar with a running counter, a divisor dial that swaps 1/4, 1/3, 1/10 and shows the count change, an inverse panel animating 20 fifths fusing into 4 wholes, a contrast switch to the partition case 1/3 ÷ 4) make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
Keep the model one-dimensional ('how many lengths fit'); adding 3D depth risks implying volume and is not needed for this concept, though this is a design judgement, not a proven limitation.
Distinguish 4 ÷ 1/5 (how many fifths in four) from both 4 ÷ 5 (dividing by the denominator) and 4 × 1/5 (four fifths); model the contrasts explicitly.

Then they lay the tiles and count to 20, and must reconcile the observation with their prediction — the gap between 'dividing makes smaller' and 20 tiles is the teachable moment.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the measurement act physically — lay 1/5 pieces into 4 wholes and count 20 together — then name the principle: a small divisor means many copies fit, so dividing by a number below 1 grows the count; contrast with 4 ÷ 5
errorPatterns.distractor: Less than 4 — dividing always makes the number smaller
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: insists the answer must be smaller than 4, or changes a correct 20 when challenged; cannot explain the bigger result

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by the denominator: reads 4 ÷ 1/5 as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, treating the unit fraction as the whole number 5

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 0.8 (or 4/5 framed as 'four divided by five'); the 1/5 is handled as '5'

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 4 ÷ 1/5. Then tell me why the answer comes out that way — is it bigger or smaller than 4, and how would you explain that to someone who thinks dividing always makes a number smaller?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely holds the measurement meaning answers 20 AND justifies it with 'how many fifths fit', comfortable that the answer exceeds the dividend. topic.name: Dividing fractions (unit fractions)
topic.description: Interpret and compute division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain the result
evidence: Compute (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 and explain using a visual model of splitting 1/3 into 4 equal parts
Create a story context for (1/6) ÷ 3 and solve it
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 1/3 of a bag of rice and splits it into 4 equal portions, can they work out what fraction of the whole bag each portion is — and explain why the answer is smaller than 1/3?

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number is the PARTITION (sharing) meaning of division: 1/3 ÷ 4 asks 'if one-third is shared among 4, how big is each part?' — splitting the third into 4 pieces cuts the whole into 3 × 4 = 12, so each piece is 1/12. This is the natural PARTNER and CONTRAST to whole ÷ unit-fraction: here the answer gets SMALLER (which matches intuition), and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely. Teach it on an area/bar model by splitting an already-shaded third, connect the double-partition (3 then 4) to the 12, and verify with the inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
bestPractices: Split a physically-shaded 1/3 into 4 equal parts on a bar and extend the cuts across the whole, so the child SEES the whole become twelfths and reads one new piece as 1/12
Make the double-partition explicit: 3 parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12 — the denominator arithmetic is the picture, not a rule
Contrast with the sibling operation (4 ÷ 1/5) so children distinguish 'share it out, gets smaller' from 'how many fit, gets bigger' — the commonest confusion in this pair
Verify every result with the inverse: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12 because 1/12 × 4 = 1/3
Use a story context ('share 1/6 of a pizza between 3') so the sharing structure is grounded
keyRepresentations: Area/bar model: a shaded 1/3 sub-divided into 4, with the whole re-ruled into 12
Number line where the 0–1/3 segment is split into 4 sub-segments of 1/12
The double-partition grid (3 × 4) tying the 12 to the two cuts
Inverse equation 1/12 × 4 = 1/3 beside the picture
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalises the just-learned 'dividing by fractions makes bigger' and inverts: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/3 × 4 = 4/3 (confuses partition with measurement division)
Gets 1/12 by a rule but cannot say why the pieces are twelfths — thinks they are still thirds
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, dividing the wrong part (e.g. 1 ÷ 4 over 3)
Adds the whole number to the denominator: 1/3 ÷ 4 → 1/7

learn.summary: Teach dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) as the sharing/partition meaning of division: 'if one-third is shared among 4, how big is each part?' Splitting the shaded third into 4 pieces re-rules the whole bar into 3 × 4 = 12 equal parts, so each new piece is a twelfth — smaller than a third. Build the double-partition (3 then 4) visually on a bar or number line, verify with the inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3, and deliberately contrast with the sibling operation (whole ÷ unit fraction, e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5) so learners distinguish 'share it out — gets smaller' from 'how many fit — gets bigger', the commonest confusion in this pair.

activities.title: Share a third four ways on a bar
feedback: If the piece is named a 'smaller third', re-extend the cut lines across the whole bar and count all 12 equal parts — the whole has been re-ruled, so the new unit is a twelfth.
If the learner cannot say where 12 comes from, point to the 3 original parts and the 4 cuts in each: 3 × 4 = 12.
Confirm by reassembling: 4 twelfths placed side by side exactly cover the original third, so 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
A number line gives the same result: the 0–1/3 segment splitting into 4 sub-segments of 1/12 mirrors the bar being re-ruled into twelfths.
activities.rationale: Partitioning the fraction into equal parts on an area/bar model or number line and justifying the result by the inverse multiplication relationship is the recommended way to model dividing a fraction by a whole number; seeing the denominator become 12 as a direct consequence of the second cut makes the computation meaningful rather than rule-bound.

Interpret and compute quotients of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division
learnerActions: Start with a whole bar that has one-third shaded.
Apply a '÷4' cut to the shaded third so it splits into 4 equal parts.

Re-rule the WHOLE bar the same way: if your cuts run along the bar (crossing the third-lines), extend them across the whole bar; if they run across the bar like the third-lines, cut each of the other two thirds into 4 equal parts too. Count: the whole is now ruled into 12 equal parts.
Read off one little shaded piece and name it: it is one-twelfth, not a smaller third.
Say out loud where 12 comes from: 3 original parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12.
Gather 4 of the twelfths back together to remake the original third, confirming 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
Optionally repeat on a number line: split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 equal sub-segments and see each is 1/12 of the whole 0–1 line.
activities.intendedInsight: Sharing one-third among 4 cuts the whole into twelfths because the second cut (into 4) multiplies the first partition (into 3): 3 × 4 = 12. The answer is smaller than 1/3, and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely — this is the picture, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Share vs. how-many-fit: the sibling contrast
feedback: If a learner inverts 1/3 ÷ 4 to 1/3 × 4 = 4/3, ask them to describe in words what is being shared and into how many parts — sharing a third cannot give each person more than a third, let alone more than a whole.
If stories are mismatched, re-read each for the action word: 'share among' signals splitting (smaller); 'how many fit' signals counting (bigger).
Re-use one bar for both questions so the two actions sit on the same picture.
activities.rationale: Over-generalising a rule that fits one operation to another is a documented interference error that instruction must confront directly; placing the two meanings on one representation and having the child state which applies targets exactly this confusion.
sourceClaims: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, and over-generalising a rule that fits one operation to another, are documented interference errors instruction must confront directly
learnerActions: Work two questions side by side on bars: 'share 1/3 among 4' (1/3 ÷ 4) and 'how many fifths fit in 4?' (4 ÷ 1/5).
For each, say aloud which action is happening: splitting one piece into more pieces, or counting how many pieces fit.
Predict before computing whether each answer is bigger or smaller than the starting number, and why.
Match short stories ('share this third between four of you' / 'how many 1/5 cups fill 4 cups?') to the correct ÷ expression.

State the rule-of-thumb in meaning terms for these cases: sharing among 2 or more makes each part smaller than the amount shared; counting how many unit fractions (smaller than 1) fit into a whole number gives an answer larger than that whole number.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (sharing) and dividing a whole number by a unit fraction (measuring how many fit) are different meanings with opposite size effects. Naming which is happening HERE prevents over-generalising 'dividing by fractions makes it bigger'.

activities.title: Build and solve your own sharing story
feedback: If a learner writes 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/9, show that sharing multiplies the parts (6 parts each cut into 3 = 18), it does not add 3 to the bottom.
If the story describes 'how many fit' instead of sharing, rewrite it so one amount is split among a number of people.
Always close by reassembling the m pieces to recover the original fraction as a check.
activities.rationale: Creating a story context and verifying via the inverse are both named practices for this objective; generating a fresh case tests transfer beyond the worked example.

Interpret and compute quotients of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division
learnerActions: Take a new case such as 1/6 ÷ 3 and write a short sharing story for it (e.g. 'share one-sixth of a pizza between 3').

Draw a bar with one-sixth shaded and split that sixth into 3 equal parts, then re-rule the whole the same way (extend cuts that cross the sixth-lines across the bar, or cut every other sixth into 3 too).
Count the total equal parts the whole is now cut into (6 × 3 = 18) and name one piece (1/18).
Verify with the inverse: 1/18 × 3 = 1/6.
Explain how you found the bottom number, referring to the two cuts, not an added-on rule.
activities.intendedInsight: The partition method generalises: for any unit fraction 1/n ÷ m, splitting each of the n parts into m re-rules the whole into n × m parts, so each piece is 1/(n×m). Whenever the fraction is shared among 2 or more (m ≥ 2) the piece is smaller than the original; sharing among 1 would leave it unchanged.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted distractors
feedback: 4/3 comes from multiplying instead of dividing (1/3 × 4 = 4/3), possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger'; but sharing a third among 4 must give something smaller than a third, so 4/3 cannot be right.
1/7 treats ÷4 as '+4 on the bottom'; sharing multiplies the parts (3 × 4 = 12), so re-cut and count the 12 pieces.
The answer 1/12 only counts as secure when the learner can name why the pieces are twelfths — if they call them 'thirds', rebuild the partition and count the 12 parts.
activities.rationale: The partition result and the bigger-vs-smaller contrast are checkable, and the specific wrong answers 4/3 (inversion) and 1/7 (added-to-denominator) map onto documented misconceptions, so they make useful distractors. A recognition item checks the result but does not by itself show the learner can construct the partition, so pair it with drawing and explanation.

learnerActions: Answer: 1/3 ÷ 4 = ? choosing from 1/12, 4/3, 1/7.
For the chosen answer, state in one sentence whether it is bigger or smaller than 1/3 and why.
On a blank bar, draw the split of a shaded third into quarters and re-rule the whole bar the same way (extend cuts that cross the third-lines, or cut each third into 4) to show the twelfths.
Answer the second-tier probe: 'Point to one small piece — how do you know it is a twelfth and not a smaller third?'
activities.intendedInsight: A secure answer is 1/12 WITH an explanation that the whole is cut more finely into twelfths; the characteristic errors are 4/3 (multiplying instead of dividing, possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger') and 1/7 (adding the whole number to the denominator).

activities.title: Talk-through sharing (optional discussion scaffold)
feedback: If the learner cannot name the piece, invite them to describe or sketch the cuts — the naming follows from counting all equal parts of the whole.
Steer talk back to 'is it bigger or smaller than a third, and why' to keep the sharing meaning central.
activities.rationale: Discussion can elicit reasoning about the sharing meaning and the size comparison, but the cutting and re-ruling that generate the twelfths need a visual surface (bar or number line), so talk complements rather than replaces the model.
learnerActions: Take on a sharing-story role: 'split this third fairly between four of you'.
Discuss aloud whether each person's piece is bigger or smaller than a third, and justify it.
Explain how the pieces get their name (twelfths) by describing the cuts you would make.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the sharing structure and the size comparison in words reinforces the partition meaning and can surface rule-following when a learner cannot name why the pieces are twelfths.

constraints: A multiple-choice or recognition item confirms the result (1/12) but does not show the learner can independently construct the partition or explain why the pieces are twelfths; pair any recognition item with drawing the split and stating the inverse.

A static or fixed bar figure can teach the partition meaning if it is read and explained, but it does not let the learner vary the sharer to generalise; include at least one case the learner partitions themselves (e.g. 1/6 ÷ 3).

The partition can also be shown on a number line (split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 sub-segments of 1/12), a representation named in the research alongside area models; offer it as an additional representation, not a replacement for the bar.

Interactive splitting (dragging a '÷4' cutter, cut lines auto-extending across the whole, auto-labelling 1/12, an inverse panel reassembling the pieces, a contrast switch to 4 ÷ 1/5) is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required mechanism.
Partitioning a fraction of a bar is a planar task; a 3D treatment is not needed here and could invite a volume misreading — kept as a noted limitation, not a claim that 3D can never help.
Always ground the answer in meaning: require the learner to state whether the result is smaller than the original fraction and why, not just produce the numeral.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12 (3 × 4 = 12) and inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3 are correct; 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/18 (6 × 3 = 18) and 1/18 × 3 = 1/6 are correct; 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20. Distractors 4/3 (inversion, from 1/3 × 4) and 1/7 (add-to-denominator) are intentional wrong answers, labelled as such, never offered as valid.
The 4/3 distractor is attributed to inverting 1/3 ÷ 4 to 1/3 × 4 (not to 4 ÷ 1/3, which equals 12); this is now stated consistently in activities 2 and 4.
Qualified the generalisation 'each piece is 1/(n×m)' so it is described as smaller than the original fraction only when shared among 2 or more (m ≥ 2); dividing by 1 leaves the fraction unchanged.

The contrast activity uses 4 ÷ 1/5 (= 20); the original row uses both 4 ÷ 1/5 and 4 ÷ 1/3 (= 12) in different fields. Both are valid 'how-many-fit' sibling cases; either is acceptable as the contrast example.

Restored the number-line representation (0–1/3 segment split into 4 sub-segments of 1/12), which the candidate had dropped; it is an alternative to the bar model and is named in the supporting IES claim.
One source claim (Common Core 5.NF.7a) is marked verified:false in the row; it is retained as cited but its verification status is unconfirmed and was not re-checked here.

The original strong claim that the partition meaning is 'FELT' only via live recompute, and that 3D 'adds nothing', has been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative necessity between media is not established by the sources provided.

probeDeeper: How is 1/3 ÷ 4 different from 4 ÷ 1/3 — which one gets bigger and which gets smaller, and why?
Point to one of your small pieces — how do you know it is a twelfth and not a smaller third?
If you shared 1/6 among 3 instead, what would each piece be, and how did you get the bottom number?
Prove your 1/12 is right using multiplication.
assess.correctAnswer: 1/12. Sharing one-third among 4 means splitting the third into 4 equal parts; cutting each third into 4 cuts the whole into 3 × 4 = 12, so each part is 1/12 — smaller than 1/3. Check: 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two meanings on one bar — 'how many fifths fit in 4' (counting, bigger) versus 'share a third among 4' (splitting, smaller) — and have the child say aloud which is happening HERE before recomputing
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/3 — dividing by a fraction makes the answer bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 4/3 (bigger than 1/3); working shows a multiplication/inversion; second tier claims the answer should be bigger

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets 1/12 but cannot justify it — says the four pieces are still 'thirds', or cannot explain where 12 comes from (rule without the double-partition meaning)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the partition physically — cut a shaded third into 4, extend the cuts across the whole, count the 12 — and connect 3 × 4 = 12 to the fraction-as-division meaning of the pieces
errorPatterns.revealedBy: First tier correct (1/12) but second tier empty or wrong: names the pieces thirds, or 'you just times the bottom by 4' with no picture

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the whole number to the denominator: 1/3 ÷ 4 → 1/7 (treats ÷4 as '+4 on the bottom')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that sharing MULTIPLIES the parts (each of 3 becomes 4, giving 12), not adds; re-cut the bar and count the total pieces rather than guessing the bottom number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 1/7; the 4 is bonded to the denominator additively

responseLevels.gap: Inverts to 4/3, or answers 1/7, or cannot start; no sharing meaning and the answer is thought to grow.
responseLevels.full: Answers 1/12 and explains it as sharing/splitting the third into 4 so the whole becomes twelfths, states clearly that the result is smaller than 1/3 and why, verifies with 1/12 × 4 = 1/3, and distinguishes it from 4 ÷ 1/3; transfers to a fresh unit-fraction ÷ whole case.
responseLevels.partial: Produces 1/12, likely by 'times the bottom by 4', but cannot picture the split or explain why the pieces are twelfths, and muddles this with the how-many-fit direction when the sibling case appears.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 1/3 ÷ 4. Then explain why, using a picture or words — what is being shared or split, and is your answer bigger or smaller than 1/3?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the partition meaning gives 1/12 AND explains it as splitting the third, naming why the pieces become twelfths (the whole is cut more finely). The telling failure is the child fresh from 4 ÷ 1/5 who over-applies 'dividing by fractions makes bigger' and inverts to 4/3 — exactly the sibling-confusion this topic must separate. The second tier also catches the child who recalls 1/12 by rule but calls the pieces 'thirds' or cannot say where 12 comes from.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Dividing unit fractions and whole numbers
topic.description: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions, using visual models and equations
evidence: Solve: '3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally — how much each?' (1/6 lb)
Solve: 'How many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups of raisins?' (6 servings)
Create a story context for a given unit-fraction division expression
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has half a pizza to share equally among 3 people, can they work out what fraction of the whole pizza each person gets — and explain the steps they took?

pedagogy.summary: This topic is the APPLICATION layer: pupils meet real contexts and must decide which unit-fraction division is happening and set it up — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The hard part is not the computation but reading the STRUCTURE: which quantity is being split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink. Teach it by modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, always sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and by having pupils invent stories for a bare expression so the structure runs both ways.
bestPractices: Model the story before the symbols: draw the sharing or the fitting on a bar/number line, then write the matching ÷ equation — IES found personalising/real contexts improves fraction-division performance
Explicitly sort the two structures — 'sharing an amount out' (partition, gets smaller) vs 'how many portions fit' (measurement, gets bigger) — and name which each word problem is
Gate every answer with estimation: 'should there be more or fewer than 2 servings?' catches a quotient pointing the wrong way
Have pupils create a story to MATCH a given expression (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5), forcing them to own the structure, not just crank a rule
Verify with the inverse operation (6 × 1/3 = 2) so the word-problem answer is checked, not trusted
keyRepresentations: Bar model of the amount being shared (partition) or filled with portions (measurement)
Number line for 'how many 1/3s fit in 2'
Story ↔ equation ↔ picture triple laid side by side
Inverse check written under the answer
commonMisconceptions: Picks the wrong operation — multiplies, or divides in the wrong order (2 ÷ 1/3 done as 1/3 ÷ 2)
Reverses dividend and divisor — computes 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 for '3 share 1/2 lb' instead of 1/2 ÷ 3
Expects the quotient to be smaller in a measurement problem, so distrusts '6 servings' being more than 2
Sets up the numbers but cannot tell which quantity is being split, so the model does not match the story

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 10-11) apply unit-fraction division to real contexts, deciding which structure a story has — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The core difficulty is reading the STRUCTURE — which quantity is split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink — not the arithmetic. Guidance centres on modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and having pupils invent stories for bare expressions so they run the structure both ways.

activities.title: Build the model, then write the equation
feedback: If you built a sharing model for a 'how many fit' story, look: the picture cannot be made to match the words — reread which quantity is the whole and which is the portion.
When six 1/3-cup scoops fill the 2-cup bar, that is 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 — count the portions in the picture to confirm.
Before trusting the number, ask 'should there be more or fewer than 2 servings?' A quotient pointing the wrong way signals a setup error.
activities.rationale: Modelling the situation before the symbols, with a visual model that matches the story, is the heart of this skill; both measurement and partition interpretations need pictures tied to the context.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
learnerActions: Read a word problem, e.g. 'How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups?'
Decide whether the story is sharing an amount out among groups (partition) or finding how many portions fit inside an amount (measurement).
Choose and build the matching model on a bar or number line: either share one bar among N people, or fill a 2-cup bar with 1/3-cup portions and count them.
Write the matching division equation (2 ÷ 1/3 = 6) once the picture matches the words.
Lay the story, the picture, and the equation side by side so the three represent the same situation.

If a digital modeller is available, dragging the story onto a bar so the equation and answer recompute live lets pupils see a mismatched picture when they pick the wrong structure — this is one helpful interaction, not a required one.
activities.intendedInsight: The story tells you which division it is: sharing an amount out among more than one group gives each less than the whole, while asking how many sub-one-unit portions fit inside an amount gives more than you started with — and the picture either matches the words or it visibly does not.

activities.title: Sort the two structures, name the dividend, then compute
feedback: If you wrote 3 ÷ 1/2 for the chocolate story, ask: what is actually being cut up and given out? The half pound — so model that amount split into 3 before writing the equation.
If you reached for 2 × 1/3, check whether the story asks you to combine amounts or to find how many portions fit — these are different operations.
A quick estimate ('more or fewer than I started with?') catches a quotient pointing the wrong way.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating partition from measurement, naming each, and then requiring a matching model is intended to confront the wrong-operation and reversal misconceptions, rather than letting pupils crank a rule.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
learnerActions: Take several word problems and classify each as 'sharing an amount out' (partition: shared among more than one group, each share is smaller than the amount) or 'how many portions fit' (measurement: when the portion is smaller than one unit, as in these problems, the count is larger than the amount).
Name, for each, which quantity is being split and which is the dividend.
For the sharing problem '3 friends share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally', identify that the half pound is what is cut up, so it is 1/2 ÷ 3, not 3 ÷ 1/2.
After classifying and naming, build the matching bar model and only then write and solve the equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the structure and the dividend first helps prevent reversing dividend and divisor and reaching for multiplication out of habit; classifying is a start, but the setup is not complete until the model and equation match the words.

activities.title: Confront 'the answer must get smaller'
feedback: If you distrusted '6 servings' because 6 is more than 2, count the scoops in the filled bar — six 1/3-cups really do fit in 2 cups.

With 3-cup servings there would be two-thirds of one serving (2 ÷ 3 = 2/3), i.e. fewer than one whole 3-cup serving fits in 2 cups; with 1/3-cup servings there are many — the portion size decides the direction.
activities.rationale: The belief that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with measurement-division problems and is best confronted with visual counting and estimation.
sourceClaims: The misconception that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with solving measurement-division word problems and must be confronted with visual counting and estimation
learnerActions: Predict, before computing, whether 'how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups' should be more or fewer than 2.
Fit 1/3-cup portions into 2 cups on a bar or number line (or with real measuring cups) and count them: there are 6.
State in words why counting portions smaller than one unit inside a larger amount gives a count bigger than the amount.
Contrast: if servings were 3-cup servings instead of 1/3-cup, would there be more or fewer in 2 cups, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A quotient can be larger than the dividend: when you count how many portions smaller than one unit fit inside an amount, the count exceeds the amount.

activities.title: Invent a story for a bare expression, then check it
feedback: If your story for 4 ÷ 1/5 is actually a sharing story or a 'four fifths' multiplication story, it does not match the division — revise it to 'how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4'.
Solve your own story back: if it does not give 20, the story does not match 4 ÷ 1/5.
Writing the inverse (6 × 1/3 = 2) under your answer checks it rather than trusting it.
activities.rationale: Creating story contexts for a given expression forces ownership of the structure, and verifying with the inverse makes the answer checked rather than assumed. Being able to invent a correct story goes beyond merely recognising one among options.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
learnerActions: Write your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve, e.g. 'How many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).
Identify which structure your story uses (here, measurement — how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4).
Solve your own story to confirm it really gives 20 and really matches division, not multiplication.
Check a given answer with the inverse operation, writing e.g. 6 × 1/3 = 2 under the answer to confirm 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Running the structure backwards — building a valid story from the symbols and verifying by the inverse — shows the structure is owned, not merely recognised.

activities.title: Talk through the direction with a context character
feedback: If your prediction and your computed answer disagree, revisit which quantity is the whole — one of them is set up wrong.
Explaining why each share shrinks (sharing) or why the count grows (fitting) shows you have read the structure, not just the numbers.
activities.rationale: A role-play dialogue set in a real context can probe 'more or fewer?' reasoning and story invention; it supplements, rather than replaces, the visual modelling where pupils build and test a setup.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
learnerActions: Take a kitchen or shop scenario where a character (cook, shopkeeper) poses a sharing problem and a portioning problem.
Before computing, predict aloud whether each answer will be more or fewer than the starting amount, and justify.
Explain to the character which quantity is being split and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the predicted direction and the dividend in a concrete context reinforces structure-reading and the 'more or fewer?' sanity check.

constraints: Matching stories to expressions and multiple-choice 'which calculation solves this?' check the choice only; classifying stories into 'sharing' vs 'how many fit' usefully targets the core difficulty (reading the structure, a source-endorsed move) but on its own does not elicit building the matching model and writing the equation. Pair classification with pupil-built models and pupil-written equations rather than treat selection alone as the whole learning.
Story invention must be produced by the pupil (constructing/writing a context), not selected from options, to reveal whether the measurement structure is owned.

A static worked pair of stories with reveal-the-setup flaps can illustrate the two structures but does not let a pupil attempt and test their own setup on a new story; treat it as a scaffold or reference.
When counting portions physically (measuring cups, cut ribbons), these are concrete approximations of the bar/number-line model; keep the link to the written equation explicit.

Contexts here are quantity and length sharing, which model naturally on a bar or number line; three-dimensional representations are not needed for these particular contexts (this is a scope note, not a claim that 3D could never help elsewhere).

Self-audit of the arithmetic: 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6; 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6; 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20; 2 ÷ 3 = 2/3 (two-thirds of one 3-cup serving); inverse check 6 × 1/3 = 2 — all consistent across the source. The common reversal error 3 ÷ 1/2 (= 6) is flagged only as an error, never offered as a valid answer or option.

The Common Core 5.NF.7c source is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited only for the standard's description of using visual models and creating story contexts, not as evidence of comparative efficacy.

No source establishes that any one artefact format is uniquely able to teach this; claims about a format being superior, or that 3D 'adds nothing conceptual', are presented as scope-limited design notes rather than established pedagogical law, and the conversation/dialogue format's efficacy is not source-established.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these two, showing your working: (a) 3 friends share half a pound of chocolate equally — how much does each get? (b) How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups? Then make up your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the SETUP separates real understanding from rule-chasing. The two problems pull in opposite directions — (a) shares an amount so the answer shrinks below 1/2; (b) counts portions so the answer grows above 2 — so a child who blindly applies one procedure gets one right and one absurd. The order of dividend and divisor in (a) exposes reversal (3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 instead of 1/6). And inventing a story for 4 ÷ 1/5 exposes whether the measurement structure is owned or only recognised — a child who writes a sharing story, or a multiplication story, reveals the gap.

pedagogy.summary: These word problems apply UNLIKE-denominator addition and subtraction in context, but their defining feature is ESTIMATION WITH BENCHMARKS (0, 1/2, 1) as a reasonableness gate. IES makes this the front-line defence against add-across: 2/5 + 1/2 cannot be 3/7, because 3/7 is less than 1/2 while the sum must EXCEED 1/2; 2/7 cannot be a plausible sum of two positive fractions that reach past a half. Teach pupils to place each fraction against a benchmark and predict the sum's region BEFORE computing with common denominators, then check the exact answer against that estimate — so an implausible result is caught, not accepted.
bestPractices: Estimate with benchmarks first — is each fraction near 0, 1/2, or 1? — and predict whether the sum is above/below 1/2 and 1 before computing (IES)
Compute exactly with common denominators, then CHECK against the benchmark estimate and reject implausible answers (e.g. a sum below 1/2 when it must exceed it)
Model on a number line marked with 0, 1/2, 1 so 'add-across gives too small an answer' is visible
Scale BOTH fractions to the common denominator (not just one) and keep the value unchanged
Use the estimate to explain WHY 2/5 + 1/2 ≠ 3/7, turning reasonableness into a habit
